docs.title: work on someone else's code
docs.text:
When work on someone else's repo (original repo), push only to our own repo, and pull updates from the original repo.

  • origin = your private repo (push here)
  • upstream = original repo (pull only)

docs.title: One‑time Setup:
docs.text:
# 1) Clone the original repo (example GIOS course project 1)
git clone https://github.gatech.edu/gios-spr-26/pr1.git
cd pr1

# 2) Point origin to your repo
git remote set-url origin https://github.gatech.edu/<gtid>/gios-spr-26-pr1.git

# 3) Add the original repo as upstream (read‑only)
git remote add upstream https://github.gatech.edu/gios-spr-26/pr1.git

# 4) Disable pushing to upstream (safety)
git remote set-url --push upstream PUSH_DISABLED

# 5) Verify
git remote -v

docs.title: Later Workflow (sync update + develop)
docs.text:
# Optional: If you have local uncommitted changes before pulling
git stash -u

# Get updates from original repo when needed
git checkout main
git pull --rebase upstream main
# Optional: keep your private repo's main in sync too
git push origin main

# Optional: If you have local uncommitted changes and ran git stash -u before
git stash pop

# Work on your code
# Create a new feature branch (Don’t develop directly on main!). Use -b only once for first creation
git checkout -b my-feature

# Push your feature branch to your private repo
git push -u origin my-feature

Then next time on same feature branch: 

git checkout my-feature
git pull --rebase
git push

docs.title: Important Notes on <cctype> Usage
docs.text:
A crucial detail for all <cctype> functions:

‼️ always cast char arguments to unsigned char‼️ before passing them to <cctype> functions, to avoid undefined behavior for non-ASCII characters. For example: std::isalpha(static_cast<unsigned char>(ch))

Reasons: - The argument passed to these functions must be representable as an unsigned char or must equal EOF. - However, on many platforms, the standard char type is signed (ranging from -128 to 127). Passing a negative char value (such as extended ASCII characters like ä, é, or 0x80–0xFF) invokes undefined behavior.

docs.title: Two Pointers
docs.text: Having two integer variables that both move along an iterable, each representing an index of the array or string, usually named something like i and j, or left and right.

docs.title: Two pointers - case 1: one input, opposite ends -> squeeze
docs.text:
Figure: Two Pointers - Case 1

Aspect Details Idea Start the pointers at the first and last indices and move them towards each other until they meet. When to use reverse array/string in place (e.g., check palindrome - after reversing, stay the same) Complexity - Time: \(\color{blue}O(n)\) (where n = arr.length) if we can keep the work inside each iteration at \(O(1)\) because the pointers start \(n\) away from each other and move at least one step closer in every iteration -> we will never have more than \(O(n)\) iterations - Space: \(\color{blue}O(1)\) because we only use two integer variables. Python For array input: 
def fn(arr):
    ans = INIT

    # Step 1. init two pointers: point to first and last element 
    left = 0     
    right = len(arr) - 1   

    # Step 2. loop: at each iteration, move two pointers towards each other, until they meet or cross (== or >)
    while left < right:  # Time: O(n)
        # do some logic here， depending on the problem

        # move two pointers closer: choose one or more from three options
        if CONDITION:  
            left += 1    # Option 1. increment the left pointer
        if CONDITION:
            right -= 1   # Option 2. decrement the right pointer
        if CONDITION:
            # do some logic here
            left += 1   # Option 3. move both pointers at the same time
            right -= 1

    return ans
For string input, extra steps: convert the string to a list before processing and join the list back to string before returning: 
def fn(s):
    arr = list(s)   # convert the string to a list
    ans = INIT

    # Step 1. init two pointers: point to first and last element
    left = 0
    right = len(arr) - 1

    # Step 2. loop: at each iteration, move two pointers towards each other
    while left < right:
        # do some logic here depending on the problem

        # move two pointers closer: choose one or more from three options
        if CONDITION:
            left += 1
        if CONDITION:
            right -= 1
        if CONDITION:
            left += 1
            right -= 1

    return ''.join(arr) # join the list back to string
C++ 
int fn(vector<int>& arr) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = static_cast<int>(arr.size()) - 1; // convert to int because std::vector::size() returns an unsigned integer type std::size_t, if arr is empty, std::size_t cannot represent -1 and will leads to a super big number

    int ans = 0;

    while (left < right) {
        // do some logic here with left and right pointers, depending on the problem
        if (CONDITION) {
            left++;
        } 
        if (CONDITION) {
            right--;
        }
    }

    return ans;
}

docs.title: Two pointers - case 2: two inputs, exhaust both
docs.text:
Figure: Two Pointers - Case 2

Aspect Details Idea start at the same first index 0, then move along both inputs simultaneously until all elements have been checked. When to use - Check subsequence - Combine two arrays Complexity - Time: \(\color{blue}O(m+n)\) (where \(m = \text{arr1.length}\), \(n = \text{arr2.length}\)) if we can keep the work inside each iteration at \(O(1)\) because at every iteration, we move at least one pointer forward, and the pointers cannot be moved forward more than \(n + m\) times - Space: \(\color{blue}O(1)\) because we only use two integer variables. Python 
def fn(arr1, arr2):
    i = j = 0   # Step 1. create two pointers: each pointer for each iterable, each start at the first index 0.
    ans = INIT

    # Step 2. loop: at each iteration, move one or two pointers forward, until one of the pointers reaches the end of its iterable (==).
    while i < len(arr1) and j < len(arr2): 
        # do some logic here depending on the problem

        # Step 3. incrementing either one of the pointers, or both. 
        if CONDITION:
            # do some logic here
            i += 1   
        if CONDITION:
            j += 1

    # Step 4. Optional: loop: iterate through the rest of the elements to make sure both iterables are exhausted, because when the above while loop finishes, one point is at the end, the other pointer might not be at the end. 
    # Note that only one of the following loops would run in reality.
    while i < len(arr1):
        # Do some logic here
        i += 1

    while j < len(arr2):
        # Do some logic here
        j += 1

    return ans
C++ 
int fn(vector<int>& arr1, vector<int>& arr2) {
    int i = 0, j = 0
    Type ans = INIT;

    while (i < arr1.size() && j < arr2.size()) {
        // do some logic here
        if (CONDITION) {
            i++;
        } else {
            j++;
        }
    }

    while (i < arr1.size()) {
        // do logic
        i++;
    }

    while (j < arr2.size()) {
        // do logic
        j++;
    }

    return ans;
}

Add/Delete Node - Singly-Linked List
docs.text:
At first, obtain the reference to the previous node prev (the node at position \(i - 1\)) by iterating from the head. Typically we do these operations on the fly, when iterating through the list (these functions are just demonstration).

Figure: Singly Linked List - insert at random position: node_to_add.next points to preNode.next, then change preNode.next points to node_to_add

Figure: Singly Linked List - Delete at random position: change preNode.next pointer to preNode.next.next

Python 
# Obtain the reference by iterating from the head - time: O(n)
def add_node(prev_node, node_to_add):   # Time: O(1)
    node_to_add.next = prev_node.next
    prev_node.next = node_to_add

def delete_node(prev_node):
    prev_node.next = prev_node.next.next
C++ 
// Obtain the reference by iterating from the head - time: O(n)
void addNode(ListNode* prevNode, ListNode* nodeToAdd) {
    nodeToAdd->next = prevNode->next;   // Time: O(1)
    prevNode->next = nodeToAdd;
}

void deleteNode(ListNode* prevNode) {
    prevNode->next = prevNode->next->next;
}

docs.text: Example: get the sum of all values from an integer linked list.

docs.title: Traverse - Iterative
docs.text:
Using dummy pointers curr without losing a reference to the head.

Python 
def get_sum(head):
    ans = 0
    curr = head

    while curr: # The final node's next pointer is null. Therefore, after the final node, the while loop ends.
        # ans += curr.val
        curr = curr.next   

    return ans
C++ 
int getSum(ListNode* head) {
    int ans = 0;
    ListNode* curr = head;
    while (curr != nullptr) {
        // ans += curr->val;
        curr = curr->next;
    }

    return ans;
}

docs.text: Figure: Doubly linked list - similar to singly linked list, but each node also contains a pointer to the previous node prev, and it allows iteration in both directions.

docs.title: Definition - Doubly linked list
Add/Delete Node - Doubly-Linked List
docs.text:
With a doubly linked list, we only need a reference to the current node at \(i\), because we can simply reference the prev pointer of that node to get the node at \(i - 1\), and next pointer of that node to get the node at \(i + 1\),

Extra work: update the prev pointers

Figure: Doubly Linked List - insert at random position: node_to_add.next points to curr_node, node_to_add.prev points to prev_node, prev_node.next points to curr_node, curr_node.prev points to curr_node

Python 
def add_node(curr_node, node_to_add):
    # get prev node reference
    prev_node = curr_node.prev  
    # relink
    node_to_add.next = curr_node
    node_to_add.prev = prev_node
    prev_node.next = node_to_add
    curr_node.prev = node_to_add
C++ 
void addNode(ListNode* currNode, ListNode* nodeToAdd) {
    ListNode* prevNode = currNode->prev;
    nodeToAdd->next = currNode;
    nodeToAdd->prev = prevNode;
    prevNode->next = nodeToAdd;
    currNode->prev = nodeToAdd;
}

Figure: Doubly Linked List - delete at random position: prev_node_next points to next_node, then change next_node.prev points to prev_node

Python 
def delete_node(curr_node):
    # get prev, next node reference
    prev_node = curr_node.prev
    next_node = curr_node.next  
    # relink
    prev_node.next = next_node
    next_node.prev = prev_node
C++ 
void deleteNode(ListNode* currNode) {
    ListNode* prevNode = currNode->prev;
    ListNode* nextNode = currNode->next;
    prevNode->next = nextNode;
    nextNode->prev = prevNode;
}

docs.title: Add/Delete First/Last node using sentinel nodes(head, tail) - Doubly-Linked lists
docs.text:
To easily add and remove at the end or tail of the linked list. No need to judge the edge cases if head or tail == nullptr

Figure: Doubly Linked List - with sentinel nodes(head, tail). Even when there are no nodes in a linked list, you still keep a head and tail. The real head node of the linked list is head.next and the real tail node is tail.prev. The sentinel nodes themselves are not part of linked list.

Figure: Doubly Linked List - with sentinel nodes(head, tail). insert at start/end

Figure: Doubly Linked List - with sentinel nodes(head, tail). delete at start/end

Python 
def add_to_start(node_to_add):
    node_to_add.prev = head
    node_to_add.next = head.next
    head.next.prev = node_to_add
    head.next = node_to_add

def add_to_end(node_to_add):
    node_to_add.next = tail
    node_to_add.prev = tail.prev
    tail.prev.next = node_to_add
    tail.prev = node_to_add

def remove_from_start():
    if head.next == tail:   # special case: empty 
        return
    # get reference
    node_to_remove = head.next  
    # relink
    node_to_remove.next.prev = head
    head.next = node_to_remove.next

def remove_from_end():
    if head.next == tail:   # special case: empty
        return
    # get reference
    node_to_remove = tail.prev
    # relink
    node_to_remove.prev.next = tail
    tail.prev = node_to_remove.prev

# create empty linked list with sentinel nodes
head = ListNode(None)
tail = ListNode(None)
head.next = tail
tail.prev = head
C++ 
void addToStart(ListNode* nodeToAdd) {
    nodeToAdd->prev = head;
    nodeToAdd->next = head->next;
    head->next->prev = nodeToAdd;
    head->next = nodeToAdd;
}

void addToEnd(ListNode* nodeToAdd) {
    nodeToAdd->next = tail;
    nodeToAdd->prev = tail->prev;
    tail->prev->next = nodeToAdd;
    tail->prev = nodeToAdd;
}

void removeFromStart() {
    if (head->next == tail) {
        return;
    }

    ListNode* nodeToRemove = head->next;
    nodeToRemove->next->prev = head;
    head->next = nodeToRemove->next;
}

void removeFromEnd() {
    if (head->next == tail) {
        return;
    }

    ListNode* nodeToRemove = tail->prev;
    nodeToRemove->prev->next = tail;
    tail->prev = nodeToRemove->prev;
}

ListNode* head = new ListNode(-1);
ListNode* tail = new ListNode(-1);
head->next = tail;
tail->prev = head;

docs.title: Reversing a singly-linked list
docs.text:
a typical problem or an intermediate step

Python 
def reverse_list(head):
    prev = None               # to track the previous node
    curr = head               # to track the current node 

    while curr:               # traverse until the tail 
        next_node = curr.next # 1. keep a reference to the original next node, make sure we don't lose it
        curr.next = prev      # 2. reverse the direction of the next pointer
        prev = curr           # 3. Update prev for the next iteration
        curr = next_node      # 4. Update curr for the next iteration

    return prev               # After the final iteration, prev points to the original tail, which is the new head

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
solve computation problems, and communicate that our solutions are correct and efficient.

Term Definition Requirements Example Define a Problem A mapping (binary relation) from problem inputs to correct outputs. - Usually don’t specify every correct output for all inputs (too many examples; one input could map to many output) - Provide a verifiable predicate (a property) that correct outputs must satisfy (so we can check whether the output is correct or not given a input-output pair) - general problem for arbitrarily large input size - Not general: small input instance: In this room, is there a pair of students with same birthday? - General: arbitrarily large inputs: Given any set of n students, is there a pair of students with same birthday? (include year, date, hour, etc.) Design Algorithms a sequence of procedure that computers will follow to solve a problem, i.e., to map each input to a single correct output - should be deterministic function, i.e., no randomness - should be correct for any arbitrary valid input. to solve birthday matching: – Maintain a record of names and birthdays (initially empty) – Interview each student in some order - If birthday exists in record, return found pair. Else add name and birthday to record – Return None if last student interviewed without success Prove Correctness - For small inputs: can use case analysis - For arbitrarily large inputs, algorithm must use induction (recursion is such a key concept) Proof of correctness of birthday matching algorithm: - Induct on \(n\): the number of students in record – Hypothesis: if first \(n\) contain match, returns match before interviewing student \(n + 1\) – Base case: \(n = 0,\) first \(0\) contains no match – Inductive steps: Assume for induction hypothesis holds for \(k\), and consider \(k + 1\). Two cases: 1. If first \(k\) contains a match, already returned a match by induction. 2. Else first \(k\) do not have match, so if first \(k+1\) has match, match contains the \(k+1\) student – Then algorithm checks directly whether birthday of student \(k+1\) exists in first \(k\) Communicate Efficiency Measure the number of operations instead of time, so that the performance of algorithms depend on the the size of input instead of underlying machine. Asymptotic Notation: ignore constant factors and low order terms – upper bounds \(O\) (worst case ) - lower bounds \(\Omega\) (best case) - tight bounds (both upper and lower, more presice) \(\Theta\) (average case) Efficient if returns in polynomial time with respect to input (not exponential)

Figure: Problem definition: mapping (binary relation, a bipartite graph) from problem inputs to correct outputs.

Aspects Details Question Under the worst case, how does runtime or memory allocation scale (upper bound), as the input size grows? Complexity Complexity is described by a math function Define Variables Variables should represent values that change between different inputs and would affect the algorithm. - If there is one input dimention, we coould define the length of an input as \(n\) - If there are multiple inputs, we could define each input size seperately as \(n, m\) or \(n = \text{length1}+ \text{length2}\) Rules Only represent when the input variables tend to infinity (sufficiently large), ignore constants and lower order terms. docs.title: Time Complexity vs Space Complexity
docs.text: Aspects time complexity space complexity Difference the amount of run time (the number of basic operations) the algorithm needs to run  relative to the input size the amount of allocated memory used by the algorithm relative to the input size trade-off which is more important depends on the specific problem. Typically, people care about the time complexity more than the space complexity. Note - ❌ never count the space used by the input (it is bad practice to operate directly on input and/or modify the input) ‼️Always ask interviewer if allowed  - ❌ usually don't count the space used by the output (the answer) unless an interviewer asks us to.

docs.title: Model of Computation : Word-RAM
docs.text:
RAM (Random Access Memory)

Aspects Definition Details Why do we need it Basis for computing efficiency: specification for what operations on the machine can be performed in constant \(O(1)\) time. CPU supports constant-time operations on an \(O(1)\) number of words (integers):– integer arithmetic: +, -, *, //, %– logical operators: &&, \|\|, !, ==, <, >, <=, >=– bitwise arithmetic: &, \|, <<, >>– Given word \(a\), can read / write at address \(a\). Computation model CPU addresses a consecutive chunk of memory (\(w\)-bit RAM cell) in constant time. The chunk size is called the word size, denoted by \(w\). A \(w\)-bit word can address \(n = 2^w\) addresses in memory. To address the largest memory address, require at least \(w \geq \log_2 n\) bits. To address more memory for arbitrarily large input, we need to increase the RAM size.

Figure: Word-RAM: Memory is an array of \(w\)-bit words. Each word is a \(w\)-bit long cell/chunk in the memory and we can access them randomly.

docs.title: Interfaces vs Data Structures
docs.text: Aspects Interface (API) Data Structures Definition A collection of supported operations a way to store non-constant data inside Random Access Memory(RAM), with algorithms that support a set of operations (called interface) on the data Exposure Level for users under the hood Key Difference a specification: what data we can store and what operations are supported and what they mean (the problem) a representation: how to store data and how operations are supported by algorithms  (the solution)

docs.text: Types Definition Order Sequence Maintain a sequence of items, \(x_0, x_1, x_2, . . . , x_{n−1}\) (zero indexing) and use \(n\) to denote the number of items stored in the data structure Extrinsic order to items (first, last, \(i\)-th) Set Maintain a set of items having unique keys (e.g., item x has key x.key) Intrinsic order to items (queries based on item keys)

docs.text: Operation Category Operation Explanation Container - build(X): given an iterable X, build new sequence from items in X - len(): return the number of stored items Staticnot change length - iter_seq() : return the stored items one-by-one in sequence order - get_at(i): return the \(i^{th}\) item \(x_i\) - set_at(i, x): replace the \(i^{th}\) item \(x_i\) with x - get_first,get_last() - set_first(x),set_last(x) Dynamicchange length - insert_at(i, x): add \(x\) as the \(i^{th}\) item. If there is a value there at index \(x\), make \(x\) the new \(x_i\). - delete_at(i): remove and return the \(i^{th}\). - insert_first(x): add \(x\) as the first item. docs.title: Sequence Data Structures: Static array vs Dynamic Array vs Linked List
docs.text: Aspect Static Array (Fixed-Size) Dynamic Array Linked List (Singly or Doubly) Memory Layout One contiguous block of memory. All elements stored sequentially. Contiguous block of memory at any given time. (same as static array) All elements are stored in nodes, scattered in arbitrary order in different locations of memory (Non-contiguous). - Singly linked list: Each node (defined by a custom class) stores not only an item value node.item but also a pointer node.next (reference to the next node, store its memory address rather than the entire node itself). * We can chain .next. * The final node's next pointer is null (None in Python; nullptr in C++). - Doubly linked list: store extra pointer node.prev to the previous node. Build Memory Allocation allocate memory for array with exact size \(n\) in \(\color{blue}\Theta(n)\) time, \(\text{space} = O(\text{time})\) Allocate extra space \(\text{size} = \Theta(n) > n\) so reallocation does not occur with every dynamic operation, only occur sometimes allocate memory for array size \(n\) Size Management 👎 Must declare fixed size and type when initialized in advance. - Everytime when the array is full, it can not store additional elements and have to reallocate a brand new array and copy values because the next word in memory might be already occupied by something else. 👍 Resize as needed - allocate a new block of memory (the exact growth factor is implementation-dependent, simplication: double the size, i.e., full ratio \(r=1/2\)), then copy data and deallocate the previous memory block automatically. - When deleting from the tail, reduce size by allocating smaller memory (still maintain the full ratio and have extra space) and copy items 👍 Number of nodes can grow or shrink arbitrarily.- Each insertion simply allocates a new node (array of size \(2\) in memory) - size is only limited by available memory. Space Usage Exact Fixed amount of contiguous memory allocated for the declared size. - May over-allocate extra unused capacity to allow future growth. - Fixed size under the hood - still need resize - In Python, list stores pointers to objects rather than objects themselves (objects themselves are separate Python objects); In C++, std::vector<T> stores objects themselves. - Each node requires pointer overhead for next (doubly linked list also needs prev plus possible allocator/object overhead.- No need for contiguous space. Check Length \(\color{blue}O(1)\) Read/Set an element 👍 Fast random access arr[i] in \(\color{blue}O(1)\) because elements (or pointers to elements) are contiguous so the location can be calculated: array[i] = memory[address(array) + i] 👍 Fast random access arr[i] in \(\color{blue}O(1)\) (same as static array). - 👎 No random access via direct indexing: to get the \(i\)-th element, must traverse from the head or tail in \(\color{blue}O(n)\). - 👍 Fast access at head: in \(\color{blue}O(1)\) because we already have a pointer to the first node (head node). - 👍 Fast access at tail: in \(\color{blue}O(1)\) if we have a pointer to the tail node. docs.title: Iterative vs Recursion
docs.text: Aspects Iterative Recursion Connection any iterative algorithm can be written recursively. Why to use it It is easier to do analysis and prove correctness on the smaller constant amount of work and info maintaining some invariant. Idea break down a problem into smaller subproblems, whose solutions can then be combined to solve the original problem. implementation - simulate repetition use for or while loops use a function that calls itself  - base case: the condition at the start of any recursive function that terminate the recursive calls.  - recurrence relation: an equation that connects solutions to subproblems. the order of code execution start at the top, and go line by line We start with the first call. In each function call, we check if it reaches base case, if so, trigger the base case and return; if not, execute the function code, then move to a next function call, the old one waits until the new one returns. The order in which the calls happens is remembered, and the lines within the functions are executed in order. When we reach the base case, return and then the recursion "moves back up" - move to the next line, return the current function, and so on, until we eventually return from the first call and the algorithm terminates.   Note that each function call also has its own local scope.

docs.text:
User - level (unprivileged) kernel - level (privileged) Definition Normal applications run here; cannot directly access hardware OS runs here; can execute privileged instructions and directly access hardware user-kernel transation - attempt when forbidden in user mode will cause a trap, application will be interrupted, hardware enforced transfer to OS, then OS decides: allow/terminate process - set a special bit in CPU = manipulating hardware is permitted; otherwise = forbidden. - OS provide system call interface for applications to invoke: e.g., open(file), send(network socket),mmap(allocate memory). - OS use signals to send notifications to the application Figure: System Call Flow

System call flow explanation:

  • Issues:

    • user → kernel → user; the context switching has overhead, not a cheap operation.
    • application performace (dependent on the ability to use cache) can benifit or suffer based on cache usage.
      • benifit: when cache contains data/address the applications needs
      • suffer: otherwise, forcing application to retrieve data from main memory. (OS bring data OS needed into cache, which replaces some application data in the cache )

  • Arguments to system call must be written by applications, it can either be passed directly from process to OS, or by specifying their address. Application must save relevant data at well-defined location.

  • Applications make a system call using specific system call number, OS can determine how many arguments it should retrive from the well defined location,

  • In synchronous mode, the process waits until the system call completes. Asynchronous modes will be talked in the future.

docs.text:
a process is an instance of an executing program, sometimes use terms "task" or "job" interchangeably with a "process"

application program → process stored on disk/flash memory/cloud, not executing (static) Once an application is launched loaded into memory and starts executing (active) If the same program (e.g., text editor) is launched more than once multiple processes will be created, they will have different state (e.g. read document_A; type in a empty new document_B ).

docs.title: What does a process look like?
Process Address Space and Memory Management
docs.text:
process encapsulates all of the data (code, the data, variables that application need to allocate) of a running application. Every element of the process state has to be uniquely identified by its address.

An operating system abstraction used to encapsulate all of the process state called address space (memory represeatation of a process), defined by a range of addresses from \(V_0\) to \(V_{max}\). Different types of process state will appear in different regions of the address space.

range Address Space (Virtual address, store process state) property \(V_{max}\) stack (e.g., save the state x before jumping to another partion of the code y, after execution of y, restore the state x) Dynamically created state that grows and shrinks as the program executes in a last-in, first-out (LIFO) order. heap (temporary results, read data from files) Dynamically created state; Seems contiguous but might not, portions of the addresses might not allocated \(V_0\) text (code), data (the data that is available when process is first initialized) static state -

Figure: Process address space, process execution example of using stack

The above address space is called virtual address, because they don't have to correspond to actual locations in the physical memory.

OS creates Page table which maintains a mapping between virtual memory addresses and physical memory addresses. By using this mapping, we decouple the complex layout of the data in the virtual address space from the layout of the data in physical memory, to maintain physical memoery management simple.

Note: It is possible for different processes to have the exact same address space range (virtual memory address range), OS will make sure that they point to distinct physical memory locations.

Example of a page table entry |veritual memory| → |physcial memory| ||:---:|--| |0x03c5||0x0f0f|

whenever the process tries to access x this page table mapping is referenced and the exact physical location where x is will be accessed.

When we do not have enough physical memory to store all the process state, the operating system must maintain information regarding processs address space to dynamically decide which portion of which process's address space will be present in physical memory and which portion will be swapped temporarily to disk, which will be brought in whenever needed.

Figure: Process 1 and Process2 in Physical memory and swap to disk

docs.title: How does OS know what a process is doing?
Process Execution State
docs.text: For an operating system to manage processes, it must have some idea about what a process is "doing". If the operating system stops a process, it must know exactly what it was doing when it was stopped, so the process can resume its execution with the exact same state.

docs.title: Process Control Block
docs.text:
the operating system maintains a process control block (PCB) data structure to maintain all useful information about Process Execution State for every single process.

The PCB is created and initialized when the process is initially created. Certain fields are updated when process state changes; other fields change frequenctly.

Operating system collect all of the data about a process - stored within CPU registers - and save it to the PCB when the process is no longer running.

- | How to maintain the process state | what information | change frequency| |--|--|--| |process state| |process number| |program counter| At any given time, the CPU use it to know where in the a instruction sequence the process currently is| every instruction, fast (maintained on CPUs' register) | |CPU registers|other information (e.g., addresses for data, status info)| |memory limit|mapping (virtual-> physical) | not too often | |a list of open file| |process priority| |signal mask| |CPU scheduling info| e.g., how much time this particular process had executed in a CPU, how much time it should allocate in the future (depends on process priority) | |stack pointer| The top of the stack (helpful to pop out the top elements of the stack) | |...| | Figure: Program Counter

docs.title: Context Switch - How is  Process Control Block (PCB) Used?
docs.text:
context switch: Each time the operating system switches the context of processes.

PCBs are stored in memory. CPU registers holds PCB value of the currently running process (which will ultimately need to be stored in its PCB) If a process is interrupted by the operating system, the operating system save its PCB (including the CPU register value). If a process is resumed, the OS restore its PCB, and update the CPU register with its PCB.

Example: Context Switch of two Processes P1 and P2 |Process P1| Operating system| Process P2| |:---:|:---:|:---:| |running ↓||idle| |interrupted|save PCB of P1, restore PCB of P2|resumed| |idle||running ↓| |running ↓|save PCB of P2, restore PCB of P1|interrupted| |running ↓||idle| context switch is expensive and we want to limit the frequency of context swtich.

  • Direct costs: the number of CPU cycles required to load and store PCB to and from memory.
  • Indirect costs: cold cache and cache misses. Specifically: When a process (e.g., P1) is running on the CPU, its data is stored in the processor cache. Accessing data from cache is much faster than from memory. When the data we need is present in the cache, we called it hot cache (process performance is at its best). When os has to context swtich to another process (e.g., P2) due to higher priority of P2 or timeout of P1, some or all of the data of P1 in the cache will be replaced for new processes P2. The next time when P1 is scheduled, its data is not in the cache (we called it cold cache) and the CPU has to spend many more time to read data from memory (cache misses).

docs.title: Process Creation
docs.text:
In operating systems, a process can create one or more child processes. The creating process is the parent and the created process is the child of that parent, share a tree-like hierarchy.

Mechanisms for process creation defination fork the operating system will copy the parent PCB into the child PCB. Both parent and child processes will execute at the same point, the instruction immediately after the fork (have same PCB including program counter). exec the operating system will take a PCB (created via fork), but will not leave the values to match the parents' value. Instead OS will replace child image and load a new program. The child's PCB will now point to values that describe this new program. The program counter of the child will now point to the first instruction of the new program. 1. call fork to create the initial process 2. call exec to replace the child's image (created in the fork) with the image of the new program. Example: Figure: Process Creation Tree

Once the initial boot process is done and OS is loaded, it will create some initial processes. When a user log into a system, a user shell process is created. When user type commands, (e.g., ls, emacs), then new processes get spawned from the shell parent process. |OS |the parent of all processes| When to start | |---|---|--| |UNIX-based OS |init | starts after system boots.| |Android|zygote| launch every new app processes|

docs.title: Role of the CPU Scheduler
docs.text:
Figure: CPU Scheduler

For the CPU to start executing a process, the process must be ready first. There might be many processes that are in the ready state waiting in the ready queue.

CPU scheduler is an operating system component that manages how processes use the CPU resources. It determines which ready process will be dispatched to the CPU to start running, and how long that process should run for.

OS must do defination preempt interrupt the executing process, save its current context run scheduling algorithem choose one of the ready processes that should be run next. dispatch dispatch process onto the CPU, and swiched into its context so the process can finally start executing. Since CPU resources are precious, the operating system needs to make sure that CPU time is spent on running processes, not executing OS operatiosn (e.g., scheduling algorithms). Therefore OS should minimize the time for perform avobe OS tasks, so OS must be efficient in the design and implementation in data structure (e.g., waiting processes,priority/history of processes) and algorithms.

docs.title: Length of Process
docs.text:
The longer we run a process, the less frequently we run CPU scheduler, the less CPU time is wasted on running CPU schduler (overhead) instead of running application processes.

Time slice: \(T_p\) denotes the time allocated to a process to run on the CPU; \(t_{sched}\) denotes the time to run CPU scheduler.

CPU usage efficiency = total processing time / total duration time

Example: If processing time is equal to the CPU schedueler time \(T_p = t_{sched}\), then CPU efficiency = 50%, only 50% CPU time spent on useful work.

Figure: CPU effiency 50%

When designing a CPU scheduler, we have to make important design decisions:

  • approporiate timeslice value
  • good metrics to choose next process to run

The process will remain in the queue until the device complete the I/O operation, then the process will move to a ready queue. running on CPU but time slice expired create a new process via fork child process executes wait for an interrupt interrupt occcurs Figure: A few ways that processes enter the ready queue.

docs.title: Inter Process Communication (IPC)
docs.text:
Many application consist of multiple processes and interract with each other to contribute to a common goal.

Example: Web application.

  • P1: Web server (front-end) accepts the customer requests.
  • P2: Database (back-end) stores customer information.

Inter process communication mechanisms (IPCs)

  • help to transfer data/information between address spaces
  • maintaining protection and isolation.
  • provide flexiblility and performance (because different types of interactions between processes exhibit different proerties).
IPC type How it works Pro + Cons - When to use Message Passing IPC Operating system establishes a communication channel, e.g., like a shared buffer. Process interact with each other by - write (send) messages to the channel. - read (recv) messages from the channel. the operating system manages this channel, providing same system calls for write/send and read/recv. overhead: Every single piece of information to be transmitted needs to be copied from user space of the sending process into the channel in the os kernel memory, and back to the address space of the receiving process. Shared Memory IPC The operating system establishes a shared memory channel, and then maps it into the address space of both processes. The processes are then allowed to directly read/write from/to this memory (the same way they can read/write from any memory as if their virtual address space). No overhead from OS: The operating system is completely out of the picture. No well-defined APIs, the usage of the shared memory is more error-prone or developers have to reimplement code. The mapping memory between processes operation is expensive If the setup cost can be amortized across a large number of messages Figure: Message Passing IPC channel between processes.

Figure: Shared Memory IPC does not have the extra channel but provides direct communication.

docs.title: Process vs. Thread
docs.text:
Aspects Process Threads Defination A single-thread process is represented by - its address space (virtual - physical memory mapping) and - its execation context (stack pointer, register, program counter etc). Threads represent multiple independent execution contexts. - shared info: They are within the same virtual address space, which means they share the virtual to physical address mapping, and the code/data/files. - Per-thread info (in a seperate data structure): Threads will potentially execute different instructions and accessing different portions of the address space, operate on different portions of the input etc. This means that each thread will have to have its own different program counter, stack stack, pointer, thread-specific registers. PCB OS represents all the information in a process control block (PCB). More complex PCB: - shared virtual address mapping, code,data - per-thread executaion context. virtual addresss seperate shared execution context ✅ ✅ context switch longer shorter communication mechanisms inter process communication (IPC) (expensive) shared variable (cheap) cache cold hot -

docs.title: Benefits of Multithreading
docs.text:
cases reasons in multi-core/multi processor system - Each thread executes same code but for different subset of input (e.g., a matrix)in parallel concurrently on a different processor to speed up - Each thread executes different portions of program for special tasks to set prioirty differently and get performance gain by hot cache why multithreading instead of multiprocess? - lower memory requirement: A multiprocess application requires more memory => more swaps from disk (we have to allocate each process a address space, and a executation context) while a multi-threaded application requires less memory (sharing address space). - lower communication overhead: communicating, passing, synchronizing data among processes (requires inter process communication IPC) is more costly than inter thread communication(shared variables in the same process address space) even on Single CPU or generally when number of threads > the number of CPUs - Hide latency associated with I/O operations: If thread has to wait on some event for some time **(t_idle)> two context switche (2*t_ctx_switch)**, then it makes sense to switch to another thread to perform other operation and switch back. - No memory overhead: Threads shared address space User applications and OS kernel support multiple execution contexts to operate concurrently - OS threads could work on behalf of apps - run OS level services like aemons and device drivers.

Figure: Multi-process requires more memory (address space) while multi-threads does not!

Figure: Multi-threading is benificial even on Single CPU

docs.title: Threads and concurrency
docs.text:
data structure and mechanisms name details thread data structure thread type all the info to represent a thread, including: Thread ID, Program counter, Stack pointer, Register values, Stack, Other thread specific attributes (e.g., for thread management) create a thread parent thread call Fork(proc, args) two arguments: - proc: the procedure that created thread will start executing - args: arguments for the procedure proc. Note that: It is not the UNIX fork. When one thread (parent thread \(T_0\)) calls fork, a new thread (child thread \(T_1\)) is created with a new thread data structure (its fields are initialized such that its program counter pointing to the first instructure of the procedure proc and the arguments will be avilable on the stack of the thread). When the thread finishes, store the results of computation in the shared address space and use mechanisms to notify the parent or other threads. terminate a thread parent thread call Join (child thread ID) The parent thread will be blocked until the child completes. Join will return to the parent the result of the child's computation. At that point,child thread exits the system and all the resources allocated for child will be freed.

Figure: Thread creation and termination

Figure: Thread creation example: insert element to a shared link list

Note: data race: because we do not know which thread will run at which time, we cannot be certain of the ordering of the elements in the shared list. Perhaps the child thread inserts its element before the parent thread, or perhaps the parent thread inserts first.

Figure: data race example: overwriting - insert element to a shared link list

If multiple threads running concurrently, the operations are randomly interleaved. Only one element will be ultimately successfully linked to the list; the other one will be lost.

docs.title: Why we need synchronization mechanisms? issues of concurrent execution
docs.text:
Figure: Data Race problem on threads because threads share memory address space

process threads Each process operate within their own address space. The operating system ensures that no valid mapping and access for any address in address space of a process (e.g., P2) to physcial memory (X) which is already mapped to another process (P1) Threads share the same virtual address space and virtual to physical address mappings, which introduces data race problems: one thread can try to read the data while another modifies it, leading to inconsistencies #### Synchronization Mechanisms To avoid the issues of concurrent execution Mechanisms Basic Idea --- --- Mutual Exclusion - mutex (like a lock) Whenever accessing shared data/state among threads: only one thread at a time is allowed to access shared data exclusively by acquiring a mutex. The other threads (blocked threads) will be suspended on the lock operation until the mutex owner releases the mutex. Note that there is no guarantee the mutex aquire requests from blocked threads will be granted in order, all of them have chances to get access to mutex. Condition Variable (used with mutex) a thread is waiting on other threads's operation with specific condition before processding. Figure: mutex example: safe insert - insert element to a shared link list

Figure: Condition Variable example: consumer and producer

  • The consumer aquire the mutex, check list is not full, then suspends itself (automatically release the mutex) and waits until the list become full (automatically aquire the mutex).
  • The producer sends signal when the list is full.

Figure: Condition Variable API Wait implementation:

docs.title: Readers/Writer Problem using condition variable
docs.text:
At any time, 0 or more readers can access the shared resource; while 0 or 1 writers can access the shared state. The readers and writer cannot access the shared state at the same time.

We can enumerate the cases, condense our two counters into one proxy variable - resource_counter. |cases|state of shared resource encoded by proxy variable resource_counter | |--|---| |if read.counter == 0 and write.counter == 0: can read, can write| free: resource.counter = 0 | |if read.counter > 0 : can read| reading: resource.counter > 0 | |if write.counter == 1 : cannot read, cannot write | writing: resource.counter = -1 (encoding as a negative number) |

Figure: Readers/Writer example implementation:

variables meaning resource_counter a proxy variable representing the state of the shared resourc. Only one thread (both reader/writer) at a time can update/access the resource counter counter_mutex a mutex which always need to be aquired whenever we access to resource_counter read_phase a condition variable signifying that the resource is ready for reading write_phase a condition variable signifying that the resource is ready for writing

Readers/Writer with proxy variable implementation - Structure

Benefit: allow more complex sharing senarios: more than one read tBenefithread or only one write thread to be in the critical section at any time. |Steps| Procedures | Details | |--|--|--| | 1| enter critical section block \(\approx\) lock | set resource_counter - the shared resource is accessed (using mutex)| | 2| critical section |read/ write shared data (no mutex)| | 3| exit critical section block \(\approx\) unlock| reverse resource_counter - free the shared resource and Singal/Broadcast condition variables (using mutex)|

Figure: critical section structure with proxy variable

docs.title: Note: When writing multi-threading
docs.text: What to do Example Write comments about which shared resource/state immediately when defining the mutex/condition variables mutex_type m_f1 // mutex for file 1 always protect access to same shared variable/operation by acquiring the same mutex. use mutex m1 for read and write file 1 Do not forget to use lock and unlock. Make sure that you are signaling or broadcasting on the correct condition. Do not use signal when broadcast are needed. The opposite is actually okay. Remember that the threads execution order is not related to the order of calling signals or broadcasts. If priority are needed, other strategies must be used. docs.title: Spurious (Unnecessary) Wake-ups
docs.text:
when we wake up threads, but the waken up threads may not be able to proceed.

Figure: Spruious Wake-up

writer readers The writer hold the counter_mutex: sending broadcast and signal readers are waiting on conditiona variable read_phase's queue The writer still holds the counter_mutex: complete the rest of operations before unlock readers are waken up and try to reacquire the mutex, but failed, so they are waiting on the counter_mutex's queue (wait again) -> waste cycles by context switching

Solution: |senarios| solutions| |--|--| |when the broadcast/signal are not depended on proxy variable| unlock the mutex before broadcast/signal| |when the broadcast/signal are not depended on proxy variable| no solution since proxy variable should be accessed within mutex lock construct | Figure: Spruious Wake-up with solution: unlock the mutex before broadcast/signal

Figure: Spruious Wake-up: no solution

docs.title: Deadlocks
docs.text:
occurs when two or more competing threads are waiting on each other to complete, but none of them ever do.

Metaphor: two stubborn workers: each grab a tool and want another tool but do not want to give up the one they have.

Figure: deadlock

A cycle in the wait graph is necessary and sufficient for a deadlock to occur. The edges are from the thread waiting on a resource to the thread owning a resource.

Thread T1 Thread T2 aquired mutex for shared resource A aquired mutex for shared resource B aquired mutex for shared resource B, but failed (since it is held by T2) aquired mutex for shared resource A, but failed (since it is held by T1) waiting waiting

Solution of deadlock: maintain same order of mutexes for each thread (hard to guarantee though)

Example: |T1| T2| |--|--| |aquired mutex for shared resource A|blocked, waiting| |aquired mutex for shared resource B|waiting| |release all mutexes | start to acquire mutexes A and then B| Deal with deadlock in real performace critical systems: |solution| meaning |cons| |--|--|--| |prevent deadlocks| Each time to acquire a mutex: check if that operation will cause a cycle in the graph: delay the operation or change code to first release some resource and afterward perform lock request | very expensive| | detect deadlocks and recover| analysis of the wait graph and determine whether any cycles have occurred.| still expensive and sometimes impossible (if input and output are external) due to rollback executation| | doing nothing| hope that the system never have deadlocks, and if we are wrong, just reboot. |

docs.title: Chapter 2: What is a Socket?
docs.text:
Topic Description Core idea A socket is a way for programs to communicate over a network using standard Unix file descriptors. Underlying Unix model In Unix, everything is a file. When Unix programs do I/O, they do it by reading or writing to a file descriptor (an integer associated with an open file). How you create a socket Call socket() to obtain a socket descriptor. How you communicate Use send() / recv() socket calls. Why it matters It gives a standard programming interface for network communication, independent of underlying hardware details.

Figure: socket metaphor : post delivery

Figure: TCP

Figure: UDP

docs.text: Item SOCK_STREAM (TCP) SOCK_DGRAM (UDP) Common name Stream socket Datagram socket Connection model Connection-oriented Connectionless by default Communication Channel Yes, reliable two-way connected communication streams. No, don’t have to maintain an open connection Error handling TCP makes sure data arrives sequentially and error-free. No. App may add its own ACK/retry logic if reliability is needed Reliability Reliable delivery Best-effort delivery Ordering Preserves order May arrive out of order Speed/overhead More overhead, generally slower Lower overhead, generally faster Typical use cases ssh, telnet, HTTP/web traffic, chat When a TCP stack is unavailable or when a few dropped packets are acceptable, e.g., tftp (trivial file transfer protocol, a little brother to FTP), dhcpcd (a DHCP client), Real-time multiplayer games, audio/video streaming, DHCP/TFTP-style workflows Key tradeoff Correctness and delivery guarantees Low Latency and throughput with possible packet loss

docs.title: Section 2.2: Network Theory
docs.text:
How packets are built:

Topic Description Encapsulation flow App data is wrapped layer-by-layer (e.g., TFTP → UDP → IP → Ethernet) before sending; receiver unwraps in reverse order and finally gets the data. Why layering helps Socket code stays mostly the same even if hardware/topology changes; lower layers abstract details away. Layered Network Model (ISO/OSI 7-layer) Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical. Layered model consistent with Unix (simplified) Application (telnet, ftp, etc) → Host-to-Host Transport (TCP/UDP) → Internet (IP/routing) → Network Access (Ethernet/Wi-Fi). Programmer responsibility Use send() for stream sockets or sendto() for datagrams; kernel/hardware handle most lower-layer header work.

Figure: Data Encapsulation

a packet is born, the packet is wrapped (“encapsulated”) in a header (rarely a footer) by the first protocol (TFTP protocol), then the whole thing (TFTP header included) is encapsulated again by the next protocol (UDP), then again by the next (IP), then again by the final protocol on the hardware (physical) layer (Ethernet).

Section 3.1: IP Addresses, versions 4 and 6
docs.text: Topic Description Example IPv4 32-bit address, decimal + dot notation 192.0.2.33 its IPv6-compatible form is ::ffff:192.0.2.33. IPv6 128-bit address, hexadecimal + colon notation, created to solve IPv4 exhaustion. shorthand: Leading zeros can be omitted and long runs of zero groups can be compressed with :: (once per address). 2001:0db8:ab00:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000 =2001:db8:ab00:: Loopback address It always means “this machine I’m running on now”. - IPv4 loopback is 127.0.0.1 - IPv6 loopback is ::1. Subnet concept Address = network part + host part, determined by a netmask (outdated). New style (Written as address/the number of network bits (can be arbitrary) in decimal for IPv4: 192.0.2.12/30, for IPv6: 2001:db8::/32 Port numbers 16-bit transport-layer endpoint identifier; same IP can host multiple services by different ports. Metaphor: Think of the IP address as the street address of a hotel, and the port number as the room number. HTTP 80, telnet 23, SMTP 25; ports <1024 are often special, and usually require special OS privileges to use.

Item Network Byte Order (Big-Endian) Host Byte Order (depends on architechture) Where it is used Standard byte order used on the wire for network protocols. docs.title: Section 5.1: getaddrinfo() — Prepare to launch
docs.text:
Functions: DNS and service name lookups, and fills out the structs we need.

We can use the results to pass to other socket functions to get our network connection established. 

#include <sys/types.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <netdb.h>

int getaddrinfo(const char *node,   
                const char *service,  
                const struct addrinfo *hints,
                struct addrinfo **res);

Parameters Description Notes *node (input) - For server: the local bind IP address - For client: the remote server target (hostname e.g. "www.example.com") or IP address) the client wants to connect to - Server setup for listening: - often set it as NULL when setting AI_PASSIVE in hints to bind()to the local host IP address. - Client: If you want to bind to a specific local IP address, drop the AI_PASSIVE in hints and put the IP address. *service (input) Port number (e.g., "80","3490") or service name (e.g., "http", "ftp, "telnet" or "smtp" etc). found in The IANA Port List1 or the /etc/services file on our Unix machine) *hints (input) pointer &hints points to a defined struct addrinfo hints that we’ve already filled out with relevant information. Example: struct addrinfo hints; hints.ai_family = AF_UNSPEC; // IPv4 or IPv6 agnostic hints.ai_socktype = SOCK_STREAM; // TCP stream sockets hints.ai_flags = AI_PASSIVE; // fill in my IP for me automatically **res (output) address of a pointer which points to a Linked list res, where each node is struct addrinfo Define pointer struct addrinfo *res and pass the address &res as output parameter int status Return value - 0 : success - non-zero : error error handling: print error using gai_strerror(status).

docs.title: Server setup code example
docs.text:
int status;
struct addrinfo hints;
struct addrinfo *res;  // a pointer will point to the results (linked list head)

memset(&hints, 0, sizeof hints); // make sure the struct is empty
// 1. Fill in struct addrinfo hints:
hints.ai_family = AF_UNSPEC;     // don't care IPv4 or IPv6
hints.ai_socktype = SOCK_STREAM; // TCP stream sockets
hints.ai_flags = AI_PASSIVE;     // fill in my IP for me

// 2. Error handling: If there’s an error (getaddrinfo() Return non-zero), we can print it out using the function gai_strerror()
if ((status = getaddrinfo(NULL, "3490", &hints, &res)) != 0) {
    fprintf(stderr, "gai error: %s\n", gai_strerror(status));
    exit(1);
}

// 3. If everything works properly: servinfo now poinst to  a linked list of struct addrinfos, each of which contains a struct sockaddr 

// ... do everything until you don't need servinfo anymore ....

freeaddrinfo(res); // 4. Free the linked-list that getaddrinfo() allocated

docs.title: Section 5.2: socket() — Get the File Descriptor
docs.text:
#include <sys/types.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>

int socket(int domain, int type, int protocol);
Parameters / Return Description Values notes domain (input) Protocol Family (PF) used by the socket. - PF_INET (IPv4) - PF_INET6 (IPv6). People used to hardcode these input values and we can still do that but using results from getaddrinfo() is better. PF_INET thing is close related to AF_INET that they actually have the same value. Use AF_INET in your struct sockaddr_in and PF_INET in your call to socket(). type (input) Communication type. - SOCK_STREAM (TCP) - SOCK_DGRAM (UDP). protocol (input) Specific protocol. - Usually 0 to auto-select the proper protocol for the given type. - Or call getprotobyname() to look up the protocol you want, “tcp” or “udp”. Return value Socket file descriptor - int sockfd on success - -1 on error The global variable errno is set to the error’s value

docs.title: code example
docs.text:
int sockfd;
struct addrinfo hints, *res;

// do the lookup
// [pretend we already filled out the "hints" struct]
getaddrinfo("www.example.com", "http", &hints, &res);

// You should do error-checking on getaddrinfo(), and walk the "res" linked list looking for valid entries instead of just assuming the first one is good. See the section on client/server for real examples.

sockfd = socket(res->ai_family, res->ai_socktype, res->ai_protocol); // Feed the values from the results of getaddrinfo() into socket() directly

docs.title: Section 5.3: bind() — What port am I on?
docs.text:
associate that socket with a port on your local machine if you’re going to listen() for incoming connections on a specific port. The port number is used by the kernel to match incoming packets to a certain process’s socket descriptor.

  • Server: usually must call bind() to claim a known local port before listen().
    • Typical server flow: getaddrinfo() → socket() → bind() → listen()
  • Client: usually skip bind() but calls connect() to connect to a remote machine.
    • The kernel’ll check if the socket is unbound, and will bind it to an unused local port automatically if necessary. 
#include <sys/types.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>

int bind(int sockfd, struct sockaddr *my_addr, int addrlen);
Parameter Description Notes sockfd (input) Socket file descriptor (fd) returned by socket(). This is the local socket you want to attach to a local address/port. my_addr (input) a pointer to a struct sockaddr that contains information about your address, namely, port and IP address Typically use res->ai_addr from res output of getaddrinfo() addrlen (input) Length (bytes) of the address passed in my_addr. Usually res->ai_addrlen Return value Result of bind operation. - 0 on success - -1 on error and sets errno to the error's value.

docs.title: Common pitfall and solutions
docs.text:
• Don’t go underboard with port numbers.
    • All ports below 1024 are RESERVED (unless you’re the superuser)!
    • You can have any port number above 1024, up to 65535 (provided they aren’t already being used by another program).
  • If bind() fails with “Address already in use”, add codes: 
    int yes=1;
//char yes='1'; // Solaris people use this

// lose the pesky "Address already in use" error message
setsockopt(listener, SOL_SOCKET, SO_REUSEADDR, &yes, sizeof yes);

docs.text:
• Typical client flow: getaddrinfo() → socket() → connect()
  • Usually no bind() needed on the client side; kernel auto-picks a local port.
#include <sys/types.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>

int connect(int sockfd, struct sockaddr *serv_addr, int addrlen);
Parameter Description Notes sockfd (input) Socket file descriptor returned by socket() serv_addr (input) Pointer to struct sockaddr (containing the destination port and IP address) Usually pass info from getaddrinfo(), i.e., res->ai_addr addrlen (input) Length in bytes of serv_addr. Usually pass info from getaddrinfo(), i.e., res->ai_addrlen. Return value Result of connection attempt. -0 on success - -1 on error and set errno.

docs.title: Section 5.5: listen() — Will somebody please call me?
docs.text:
listen() wait for incoming connections and handle them.

int listen(int sockfd, int backlog);
Parameter Description Notes sockfd (input) Socket file descriptor (fd) returned by socket() system call. backlog (input) the limit about number of connections allowed waiting in the incoming queue until you accept(). Most systems silently limit this number to about 20; you can probably get away with setting it to 5 or 10. Return value Result of listen setup. - 0 on success - -1 on error and sets errno on error.

docs.text:

socket();
bind();
listen();
// accept() goes there
  • Call bind() before listen() so that the server is running on a specific port and then clients know which port to connect to.

docs.title: Section 5.6: accept() — “Thank you for calling port 3490.”
docs.text:
accept() pulls one pending client connection from the listen queue and Return a new socket descriptor for that connection.

  • The original sockfd (listening socket) keeps listening for new client connections.
  • The returned new_fd is the socket ready to send() / recv() with this specific client.
  • If your server only needs one connection, you can close() the listening socket after accept() to prevent more incoming connections on the same port.
#include <sys/types.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>

int accept(int sockfd, struct sockaddr *addr, socklen_t *addrlen);
Parameter Description Notes sockfd (input) Listening socket descriptor. addr (output) a pointer to a local struct sockaddr_storage - Define struct sockaddr_storage their_addr; - cast it to (struct sockaddr *) by (struct sockaddr *)&their_addr struct sockaddr_storage is where the information about the incoming connection will go (and with it you can determine which host is calling you from which port). addrlen (input) a local integer variable that should be set to sizeof(struct sockaddr_storage) before its address is passed to accept() addr_size = sizeof their_addr; Return value A new connected socket descriptor. - new_fd >= 0 on success - -1 on error and sets errno.

docs.text:
s#include <string.h>
#include <sys/types.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <netdb.h>

#define MYPORT "3490"  // the port users will be connecting to
#define BACKLOG 10     // how many pending connections queue holds

int main(void)
{
    struct sockaddr_storage their_addr; // for setting *addr
    socklen_t addr_size; // // for setting *addrlen

    struct addrinfo hints, *res;
    int sockfd, new_fd;

    // !! don't forget your error checking for these calls !!

    // load up address structs with getaddrinfo():
    memset(&hints, 0, sizeof hints);
    hints.ai_family = AF_UNSPEC;  
    hints.ai_socktype = SOCK_STREAM;
    hints.ai_flags = AI_PASSIVE;     

    getaddrinfo(NULL, MYPORT, &hints, &res);

    // make a socket, bind it, and listen on it:
    sockfd = socket(res->ai_family, res->ai_socktype,
                                                 res->ai_protocol);
    bind(sockfd, res->ai_addr, res->ai_addrlen);
    listen(sockfd, BACKLOG);

    // Accept an incoming connection:
    addr_size = sizeof their_addr;
    new_fd = accept(sockfd, (struct sockaddr *)&their_addr,
                                                       &addr_size);

    // ready to communicate on socket descriptor new_fd!

docs.title: Section 5.7: send() and recv() — Talk to me!
docs.text:
send() and recv() are for data transfer on stream sockets (TCP) or connected datagram sockets.

  • For unconnected datagram sockets (UDP), use sendto() / recvfrom() instead.

They are blocking calls:

  • recv() will block (sleep) until there is some data ready to receive.
  • send() can also block if the stuff you’re sending is all jammed up somehow, but that’s rarer. 
int send(int sockfd, const void *msg, int len, int flags); 
int recv(int sockfd, void *buf, int len, int flags);
send() Parameter / Return Description Notes sockfd (input) Socket descriptor to send data to. Can be a connected socket returned by socket() or the new_fd returned by accept(). msg (input) a pointer to the data you want to send Example: char *msg = "Your message"; len (input) the length of that data in bytes. Usually strlen(msg) for strings (without \0). flags (input) Send flags. set to 0. Return value Number of bytes actually sent. -1 on error and errno is set to the error number. Note: may send fewer bytes than requested. If the value returned by send() (actually sent) doesn’t match the value in len (intend to send), it’s up to you to send the rest of the string by looping until all bytes are sent. If the packet is small (less than 1K or so) it will probably manage to send the whole thing all in one go. recv() Parameter / Return Description Notes sockfd (input) Socket descriptor to receive data from. Usually connected stream socket. buf (output) buffer to read the information into Must have enough allocated memory. len (input) maximum length of the buffer buf. Protects against buffer overflow flags (input) Receive flags. set to 0. Return value Number of bytes actually received into buffer. - -1 on error (errno set) - 0 means remote side closed the connection.

docs.title: Section 5.9: close() and shutdown()
docs.text:
After communication is done, use these calls to stop socket I/O.

  • close() closes the socket file descriptor completely.
    • Prevents further reads/writes
    • frees descriptor resource.
  • shutdown() disables communication in certain direction(s). More control than close().
    • but does not free the socket descriptor (need to call close() to fully free it).
close(sockfd);

int shutdown(int sockfd, int how);
Parameters Description Meaning sockfd (input) the socket file descriptor you want to shutdown 0 on success, -1 on error (errno set). how (input) disable direction control - 0: Further receives are disallowed. - 1: Further sends are disallowed. - 2: Further sends and receives are disallowed (similar communication effect to close()). Return value shundown result - 0 on success - -1 on error (errno set)

docs.title: code examples
docs.text:
// fully close socket:
close(sockfd);

// or selectively disable communication first:
shutdown(sockfd, 1);  // no more sends
close(sockfd);        // finally release descriptor

int getpeername(int sockfd, struct sockaddr *addr, int *addrlen);

Socket must already be connected. addr (output) a pointer to astruct sockaddr or struct sockaddr_in that will hold the information about the other side of the connection addrlen (input) a pointer to an int should be initialized to sizeof *addr or sizeof(struct sockaddr Return value Result of query. - 0 on success - -1 on error and sets errno accordingly

docs.title: Chapter 6: Client-Server Background
docs.text:
Client processes and server processes communicate in request/response style over the network. Note that the client-server pair can speak SOCK_STREAM, SOCK_DGRAM, or anything else (as long as they’re speaking the same thing).

Figure: Client-Server Interaction

aspects Client (multiple) (metaphor: caller) Server (only one) (metaphor: public phone line) Role Initiates connection to a server and requests data/service. listens on a known port, waits for incoming connections and responds to clients. Model Parent process keeps waiting for a connection, accept() it, then fork() a child process to handle each client. Socket - sockfd listening socket (stays open) - new_fd: connected socket for one client Typical stream flow resolve server address getaddrinfo() -> create socket socket() -> call server connect() -> receive reply recv() -> close socket getaddrinfo() -> socket() -> bind() -> listen() -> accept()

docs.title: Section 6.1: A Simple Stream Server
docs.text: This demo server accepts TCP connections and sends "Hello, world!" out over the stream connection.

docs.title: minimal server code example
docs.text:
/*
** server.c -- a stream socket server demo
*/

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <errno.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <sys/types.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <netinet/in.h>
#include <netdb.h>
#include <arpa/inet.h>
#include <sys/wait.h>
#include <signal.h>

#define PORT "3490"  // server listens on this TCP port,clients will be connecting to this port

#define BACKLOG 10   // maximum pending connections queue will hold

void sigchld_handler(int s)
{
    (void)s; // quiet unused variable warning

    // waitpid() might overwrite errno, so we save and restore it:
    int saved_errno = errno;

    while(waitpid(-1, NULL, WNOHANG) > 0);

    errno = saved_errno;
}


// get sockaddr, IPv4 or IPv6:
void *get_in_addr(struct sockaddr *sa)
{
    if (sa->sa_family == AF_INET) {
        return &(((struct sockaddr_in*)sa)->sin_addr);
    }

    return &(((struct sockaddr_in6*)sa)->sin6_addr);
}

int main(void)
{
    // listen on sock_fd, new connection on new_fd
    int sockfd, new_fd;
    struct addrinfo hints, *servinfo, *p;
    struct sockaddr_storage their_addr; // connector's address info
    socklen_t sin_size;
    struct sigaction sa;
    int yes=1;
    char s[INET6_ADDRSTRLEN];
    int rv;

    memset(&hints, 0, sizeof hints);
    hints.ai_family = AF_INET;
    hints.ai_socktype = SOCK_STREAM;
    hints.ai_flags = AI_PASSIVE; // use my IP

    if ((rv = getaddrinfo(NULL, PORT, &hints, &servinfo)) != 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "getaddrinfo: %s\n", gai_strerror(rv));
        return 1;
    }

    // loop through all the results and bind to the first we can
    for(p = servinfo; p != NULL; p = p->ai_next) {
        if ((sockfd = socket(p->ai_family, p->ai_socktype,
                p->ai_protocol)) == -1) {
            perror("server: socket");
            continue;
        }

        if (setsockopt(sockfd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_REUSEADDR, &yes,
                sizeof(int)) == -1) {
            perror("setsockopt");
            exit(1);
        }

        if (bind(sockfd, p->ai_addr, p->ai_addrlen) == -1) {
            close(sockfd);
            perror("server: bind");
            continue;
        }

        break;
    }

    freeaddrinfo(servinfo); // all done with this structure

    if (p == NULL)  {
        fprintf(stderr, "server: failed to bind\n");
        exit(1);
    }

    if (listen(sockfd, BACKLOG) == -1) {
        perror("listen");
        exit(1);
    }

    sa.sa_handler = sigchld_handler; // reap all dead processes
    sigemptyset(&sa.sa_mask);
    sa.sa_flags = SA_RESTART;
    if (sigaction(SIGCHLD, &sa, NULL) == -1) {
        perror("sigaction");
        exit(1);
    }

    printf("server: waiting for connections...\n");

    while(1) {  // main accept() loop
        sin_size = sizeof their_addr;
        new_fd = accept(sockfd, (struct sockaddr *)&their_addr,
            &sin_size);
        if (new_fd == -1) {
            perror("accept");
            continue;
        }

        inet_ntop(their_addr.ss_family,
            get_in_addr((struct sockaddr *)&their_addr),
            s, sizeof s);
        printf("server: got connection from %s\n", s);

        if (!fork()) { // this is the child process
            close(sockfd); // child doesn't need the listener
            if (send(new_fd, "Hello, world!", 13, 0) == -1)
                perror("send");
            close(new_fd);
            exit(0);
        }
        close(new_fd);  // parent doesn't need this
    }

    return 0;
}

docs.title: Section 6.2: A Simple Stream Client
docs.text: This demo client connects to the host we specify on the command line, port 3490, receives the string the server sends.

docs.title: minimal client code example
docs.text:
/*
** client.c -- a stream socket client demo
*/

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <errno.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <netdb.h>
#include <sys/types.h>
#include <netinet/in.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>

#include <arpa/inet.h>

#define PORT "3490" // the port client will be connecting to 

#define MAXDATASIZE 100 // max number of bytes we can get at once 

// get sockaddr, IPv4 or IPv6:
void *get_in_addr(struct sockaddr *sa)
{
    if (sa->sa_family == AF_INET) {
        return &(((struct sockaddr_in*)sa)->sin_addr);
    }

    return &(((struct sockaddr_in6*)sa)->sin6_addr);
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    int sockfd, numbytes;  
    char buf[MAXDATASIZE];
    struct addrinfo hints, *servinfo, *p;
    int rv;
    char s[INET6_ADDRSTRLEN];

    if (argc != 2) {
        fprintf(stderr,"usage: client hostname\n");
        exit(1);
    }

    memset(&hints, 0, sizeof hints);
    hints.ai_family = AF_UNSPEC;
    hints.ai_socktype = SOCK_STREAM;

    if ((rv = getaddrinfo(argv[1], PORT, &hints, &servinfo)) != 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "getaddrinfo: %s\n", gai_strerror(rv));
        return 1;
    }

    // loop through all the results and connect to the first we can
    for(p = servinfo; p != NULL; p = p->ai_next) {
        if ((sockfd = socket(p->ai_family, p->ai_socktype,
                p->ai_protocol)) == -1) {
            perror("client: socket");
            continue;
        }

        inet_ntop(p->ai_family,
            get_in_addr((struct sockaddr *)p->ai_addr),
            s, sizeof s);
        printf("client: attempting connection to %s\n", s);

        if (connect(sockfd, p->ai_addr, p->ai_addrlen) == -1) {
            perror("client: connect");
            close(sockfd);
            continue;
        }

        break;
    }

    if (p == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "client: failed to connect\n");
        return 2;
    }

    inet_ntop(p->ai_family,
            get_in_addr((struct sockaddr *)p->ai_addr),
            s, sizeof s);
    printf("client: connected to %s\n", s);

    freeaddrinfo(servinfo); // all done with this structure

    if ((numbytes = recv(sockfd, buf, MAXDATASIZE-1, 0)) == -1) {
        perror("recv");
        exit(1);
    }

    buf[numbytes] = '\0';

    printf("client: received '%s'\n",buf);

    close(sockfd);

    return 0;
}

docs.title: Control Flow: if, elif, and else

Keyword Logic Efficiency if Starts a conditional block. Always evaluated. elif "Else if" making the conditions mutually exclusive - checked only if preceding if/elif were False. Increases efficiency by avoiding unnecessary checks when preceding if/elif were True. else A "catch-all" default outcome for any case not met by if or elif. No need to evaluate the last case ### Template
