docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
Course source: CS50P Lecture 03

Handle something out of the ordinary (exceptional). All errors in Python are dealt with using exceptions, but not all exceptions are errors.

docs.title: Error Categories
docs.text: Error Type Definition When to be Caught Example Solution Syntax Error Errors in the "grammar" of the code. caught before the program runs - Missing quotes, unclosed parentheses (unterminated: started something but didn't stop it; literal:something we literally typed) - Typos Double-check typing; the interpreter usually points to the line. Runtime Error Errors that occur while the program is running due to unexpected behavior. caught during execution. - Unexpected user input (ValueError: e.g., entering "cat" when a number is expected). Implement "defensive programming" using try-except blocks.

docs.title: Use try/except block to catch errors
docs.text:
These keywords allow you to try to run some code except if something goes wrong, to handle errors caused by unexpected events gracefully without crashing.

Keyword Defination Behavior Purpose Note try Try to execute a block of code that might cause errors. If the whole block of code executes without any run-time errors, just run the code after the try-except block (e.g., else block if it exists). testing out code before something goes wrong - Only include the fewest lines of code possible that are likely to fail (because the error will be catched immediately and then the program skip the rest of the try block and jump to except block) - combine with while loop** when handling incorrect user input: ask for input again. except Defines the code to run to handle the error if a specific error occurs in the try block. Prevents the program from crashing by allowing a defined response to errors. - It is a bad practice to catch all runtime error in one except using except Exception: - Better practice: figure out what kind of errors could happen and handle them seperately explicitly. else Defines code to run if no exceptions were raised in the try block. For logic that depends on the successful execution of the try block. Keyword Purpose Behavior pass Silently ignores an exception. Acts as a null placeholder. The program will catch the error but take no action Execution continues to the next line of code immediately following the current block. continue Interrupts the current loop iteration. Jumps directly back to the top of the loop (the while True line) and starts a new cycle

docs.title: Syntax template - try-except block
docs.text:
try:
    # Fewest lines of code that might raise errors
except SpecificErrorType:
    # Handle the specific type of error or simply pass the error without handling it
else:
    # code to run when there is no error raised

Note: The exception code can access a variable that contains information about exactly what the error was. Example: 

try:
    items = ['a', 'b']
    third = items[2]
    print("This won't print")
except Exception as e: # specify a variable name e then the exception clause code can refer to that variable name.
    print("got an error")
    print(e) # print out the information that would normally be printed as an error message

print("continuing")

docs.title: Example Implementation
docs.text:
The get_int Function demonstrates the "Pythonic" way to ensure a user provides a valid input integer without crashing the program.

def main():
    # Pass the prompt as an argument for flexibility
    percentage = get_valid_fraction("Fraction: ")
    print(f"Fuel level: {percentage:.0%}")

def get_valid_fraction(prompt):
    while True:
        fraction = input(prompt)
        try:
            # Attempt parsing and conversion
            x_str, y_str = fraction.split("/") 
            percentage = int(x_str) / int(y_str)
        except (ValueError, ZeroDivisionError): 
            # Handle non-integers or division by zero by re-prompting
            continue
        except EOFError:
            # Move to a new line and exit when user hits Control-D
            print()
            break
        else:   # If the user enters a input in correct format, further validate it here
            if 0 <= percentage <= 1:
                return percentage
            # Otherwise, re-prompting again for invalid logic
            continue

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Common Error Type
docs.text:
Understanding specific error names allows us to target error handling.

All exceptions are objects. The classes that define the objects are organized in a hierarchy - the parent class of a set of related exceptions will catch all exception messages for itself and its child exceptions. For example, an ArithmeticError exception will catch itself and all FloatingPointError, OverflowError, and ZeroDivisionError exceptions.

Exception Meaning Common Scenario ValueError A function receives an argument of the right type but inappropriate value. Using int() on a string that isn't a numeric integer, e.g., int("1.5"), int("three"), int("cat"). NameError Attempting to use a variable that has not been defined. Accessing x after the line x = int(input()) failed and skipped assignment. ZeroDivisionError The second argument of a division or modulo operation is zero Calculating percentage x/y when the denominator y is 0 KeyError Attempting to access a dictionary key that does not exist access dictionary using dict[key] instead of .get() EOFError "End of File" error, occurs when the user inputs Control-D Used as a standard way for a user to signal they are finished with input FileNotFoundError Raised when a file or directory is requested but does not exist. Attempting to open or read a file that is not in the current directory. IndexError Occurs when attempting to access an index that is outside the bounds of a list. Accessing list index but index is out of range, e.g.,sys.argv[1] when the user forgot to provide a command-line argument. requests.RequestException The base class for all exceptions raised by the requests library. A "catch-all" to prevent a crash if an API query fails due to network or connection issues. AssertionError Raised when an assert statement's boolean condition evaluates to False. Raised during unit testing when checking if a function's returned value is not equal to its expectations

docs.title: When to Use Exception
docs.text:
• Error Handling:
    • Handle Common Error Exceptions:
    • Graceful Degradation: Allow the program to continue running with reduced functionality rather than crashing.
  • Cleanup Resource:
    • Ensure resources such as files, network connections, or hardware interfaces are properly closed or released in the event of an error.
  • Graceful Shutdown when users Interrupt:
    • Handle user-generated interrupts (e.g., KeyboardInterrupt) to shut down processes cleanly, providing feedback to the user
  • Maintain robustness of Long-Running Processes:
    • involving loops, sleep methods, or long-running tasks by handling potential interruptions or errors.

docs.title: Use raise to manually trigger an error
docs.text:
There is a whole suite of exceptions that already exist and we can also create our own error types.

Keyword When to Use Behavior Syntax Example raise Alter programmers and users when something is wrong or they use it in an incorrect way. Manually triggers a specific exception. raise SpecificErrorType("ErrorMessage") raise ValueError("Invalid age")

docs.title: Why use raise?
docs.text:
• Enforce Our Own Logic: Python doesn't mind if an age is -5, but your program should.
  • Better Debugging: It provides specific error messages that help you find bugs faster.

docs.title: Example Implementation
docs.text:
def main():
    user_age = get_age()

def get_age():
    age = int(input("Age: "))
    if age < 0:
        # Trigger an error manually
        raise ValueError("Age cannot be negative!")
    return age

main()

docs.title: Packages & APIs: requests & json
docs.text:
Third-party packages (installed via package manager pip install package_name) allow us to interact with external data and functionalities. PyPI is a repository or directory of all available third-party packages currently available.

APIs (application program interfaces) refer to third-party services that we can write code to connect to download and access data. requests is a package that allows our program to make internet request using python code behave as a web browser. We can constructe URL by reading the API documentation we request.

The format in the downloaded text file is called JSON (javascript object notation) , a language agnostic text-based format that is used to exchange text-based data between applications. Python has a built-in json library that can help us interpret the data received.

Method Purpose Syntax Parameter Return Value requests.get() Download data from a URL and store it into response object, like typing url in a web browser and enter. response = requests.get(url) url: The https url to the API in string format. Check the documentation of the API. Response object response.json() Converts that JSON response into a Python dictionary so that we can extract specific information content = response.json() dict or list json.dumps() Format JSON data for nice printing. json.dumps(obj, indent=2) - obj - indent: Indentation making nested data more readable. str

Best practice: using try-except block for requests:

get.py 

import requests

def get_item(query):
    payload = {'key1': 'value1', 'key2': ['value2', 'value3']}
    try:
        response = requests.get(
            "https_url",
            params = payload
        )
        response.raise_for_status()  # will raise an HTTPError if the HTTP request returned an unsuccessful status code.
    except requests.RequestException:
        print("Couldnt complete request!")
        return []

    content = response.json()
    return [item["key"] for item in content["data"]]

docs.text:
The FPDF class is the primary engine for creating and exporting PDF documents.

The canvas uses a standard 2D millimeter-based coordinate system

  • Origin \((0,0)\): Located at the top-left corner of the PDF page
  • \(X\)-Axis (Horizontal): Measures distance from the left edge (\(0\text{ mm}\)) to the right edge (\(210\text{ mm}\)).
  • \(Y\)-Axis (Vertical): Measures distance from the top edge (\(0\text{ mm}\)) down to the bottom edge (\(297\text{ mm}\)).
  • Internal Cursor: fpdf2 maintains an internal drawing cursor \((x, y)\) that tracks where the next text or image will be placed automatically unless we override it.
Method / Constructor Purpose Syntax Example Parameters / Options Return Value / Behavior FPDF() Constructor Instantiates a new PDF document object with page dimensions and units. pdf = FPDF(orientation="P", unit="mm", format="A4") - orientation: "P" (Portrait) or "L" (Landscape) or "Letter", Legal. - unit: Measure unit ("mm", "cm", "pt", "in").- format: Standard page sizes ("A4" = 210x297mm). Returns a new FPDF instance. pdf.add_page() Adds a new blank page to the PDF document. The origin is at the upper-left corner and the current position is by default placed at 1 cm from the borders; the margins can be changed with set_margins. pdf.add_page() None. Appends a page pdf.set_font() Before we can print text, it is mandatory, otherwise the document would be invalid. pdf.set_font("helvetica", style="B", size=30) - family: Built-in fonts ("helvetica", "times", "courier", Symbol and ZapfDingbats).- style: "" (Regular), "B" (Bold), "I" (Italic), "U" (Underline).- size: Font size in points (pt). Updates active document font settings. pdf.set_text_color() Sets the foreground text color using RGB or grayscale values. pdf.set_text_color(255, 255, 255) - RGB: Three integers (0–255) for Red, Green, Blue (e.g., 255, 255, 255 for white).- Grayscale: Single integer (0–255). docs.text:
Course source: CS50P Lecture 05

Best practice: write a little extra code to test the code we wrote, testing individual units or functions.

docs.title: Manual Testing vs Unit Testing
docs.text:
Concept Description Typical Pattern / Command Key Takeaway Manual Testing Running your program manually and typing in inputs to check if the outputs are correct. python filename.py Slow, error-prone, and doesn't scale as codebases grow. Unit Testing (best practice) Writing separate program(s) that call your individual functions with specific inputs and test if the returned values match expectations. python test_filename.py Most common in industry; allows you to automate testing and catch "corner cases".

Note: Ensuring if __name__ == "__main__": main() so that testing file or program don't execute the main() in the tested file when imported.

docs.title: Keyword assert
docs.text:
The assert statement claims a boolean expression is true. If the boolean expression is true, nothing will happen; if the expression is false, Python raises an AssertionError.

Feature Syntax Behavior on Failure Example Basic Assert assert boolean_expression Raises AssertionError and halts execution of subsequent tests in that function. assert square(2) == 4 Assert with Message assert condition, "Error Msg" Raises AssertionError displaying the custom error message. assert square(2) == 4, "2 squared was not 4" Catching AssertionError try: ... except AssertionError: Catch the failure for the test cases to log details without crashing the testing script. try: assert square(2) == 4 except AssertionError: ...

docs.title: Why assert alone can be bloated:
docs.text: Using manual try...except AssertionError blocks for dozens of test cases makes your testing code extremely bloated and repetitive. This is why automated third-party frameworks like pytest are used to handle these try...except AssertionError blocks.

docs.title: Automated Testing with pytest
docs.text:
pytest is a popular third-party testing framework that automates running unit tests and provides detailed, structured reports on which tests passed or failed. Based on the results of the test, we can go correct our code.

Command Purpose Syntax / Action Notes Installation Installs the pytest package from PyPI. pip install pytest Run once in your terminal. Run Single File Runs all functions prefixed with test_ in the specified test file. pytest test_filname.py Displays a summary of passes (green dots .) and failures (red F) with the red E providing hints about the errors detailed traceback. Dividing Tests Break each original function into smaller bite-sized functions and write separate test_function(). Divide one test_function() into different groups of tests def test_function_groupname(): assert function(input) == true_value pytest runs every test function; a failure in one won't stop others from running so that more errors are being displayed allowing us to further explore the bugs. Testing Exceptions Express we expect a specific error to be raised when running the block. import pytest def test_function():with pytest.raises(ErrorType): # code that should raise the exception Requires import pytest at the top of the testing file. Function Purpose Syntax Parameters Return Value Common Scenario pytest.approx() Compare floating-point numbers safely with approximated value by allowing a small margin of error (tolerance) to bypass binary precision limitations. pytest.approx(expected, abs=None) - expected: The number (or list/dictionary of numbers) you expect. - abs (Optional): Absolute tolerance (maximum allowed difference). Set this tolerance based on specifications first; do not expand it just to force a failing test to pass. An approximation wrapper object that handles the margin of error calculations during comparisons. Testing float calculations where minor rounding issues occur

docs.title: Example: Testing Returns and Exceptions
docs.text:
import pytest
from calculator import square

# Testing different groups e.g., positive, negative, zero
def test_positive():
    assert square(2) == 4
    assert square(3) == 9

def test_negative():
    assert square(-2) == 4
    assert square(-3) == 9

def test_zero():
    assert square(0) == 0

def test_float():
    assert square(0.231) == pytest.approx(0.0536, abs = 1e-5)

docs.title: File I/O
docs.text:
Course source: CS50P Lecture 06

File I/O (Input/Output) allows programs to read from and write to files, enabling persistent storage so that data is not lost and can be used later when the program ends.

docs.title: Opening a File
docs.text:
Best practice: using with keyword to open a file-like object at the filepath, write some content and automatically safely closes after exit this code block even if exceptions occur inside the block.

with open(filepath, mode) as file:
    # Use the file-like object file

  • filepath: "/path/file_name.file_extension" (or simplely "file_name.file_extension" if it is in the current path)

  • mode (optional)

  • as file: the name of the variable that should be assigned the return value of open
  • we can actually open multiple files at once (use case: read one file and write another at the same time) 
    with open(filepath, mode) as file_1, open(filepath, mode) as file_2:
    # Use the file-like object file

docs.text: Mode Syntax Purpose If the File Exist or Not Write "w" Write fresh content or overwrite an existing file. create the file if missing. However, if the file does exist, it will clear any existing content before writing new data. Safe Create "x" create a new file only if it does not exist Raise FileExistsError if the file already exists to prevent accidental overwrites. (handle it via try-except block) Append "a" Append data to the end of the file without deleting existing content. create the file if missing Read "r" Read (default mode). Raise an error FileNotFoundError Both read and write "+" combine with other modes (e.g., "r+", "w+") for both reading and writing

var = input("prompt string")

docs.title: Read Mode
docs.text:
with open(filepath, "r") as file:  
    for line in file:   # Iterates through line-by-line. If we want the lines to be sorted, we can use sorted(file)
        print(line.rstrip())  # Removes extra trailing line break to prevent double new line issues caused by the file's `\n` and `print()`'s default newline.
If we want to further change the data, e.g., sorting, we can create a variable at the top, append info to collect it in one place. Example:

docs.title: Writing Text Files
docs.text: Method Purpose Syntax Parameters Return Value Pros &Cons When to Use write() Writes a string to the end of the file. file.write(string) string: The text string to write. It does not automatically add newlines so we must append manually. Building a single string and calling write() once, i.e., text = " ".join(lines) + " " can be more efficient and less error-prone compared to writelines(). None + Safe and predictable. - Cannot write lists/iterables natively without manual conversion. Best for writing individual strings or custom-formatted blocks. writelines() Writes each line as an item in a list (or any iterable sequence) of strings to the end of the file. file.writelines(list) list: A list or iterable of strings. It does not add newlines automatically we must include in each string in the list. None + Dumps an entire sequence of lines in a single call.- Highly error-prone. Beginners often forget that it doesn't auto-add newlines, resulting in all list items squished onto a single line. Use when you already have a pre-formatted list of strings that already contain newline characters at the end.

docs.title: Reading Text Files
docs.text:
Method Purpose Syntax Parameters Return Value Pros &Cons When to Use Direct Iteration Iterate line-by-line for line in file: None Yields a string representing one line at a time. + Extremely memory-efficient. Only keeps one line in RAM at a time (perfect for massive files).- Cannot access lines out of order (no indexing or slicing). Default best practice for standard line-by-line file processing. read() Reads n characters, or the entire file as a single string if n is omitted. file.read(n=-1) - n (Optional): The number of characters to read. Defaults to -1 (reads the entire file). A string containing all the read characters. + Gives you the entire file as one easily searchable string.- Poor memory efficiency for large files; loads the entire file into RAM at once. When we need to process small files as a single block (e.g., parsing JSON/XML) or searching for substrings across line boundaries. readline() Reads the next line of the file with all text up to and including the newline character. file.readline(n=-1) n (Optional): Maximum characters to read from the line. If n is provided as a parameter, then only n characters will be returned if the line is longer than n. (Note: Parameter n is ignored in the browser version of Python and is rarely used). A string containing the next line of tex (includes ). Returns an empty string "" when the end of the file is reached. + Great for grabbing a specific single line (e.g., reading a header line before starting a loop to process data). - Clunky if you just want to loop through the whole file. When you need precise, manual control over step-by-step reading. readlines() Read all the lines of the file lines = file.readlines() n (Optional): If n is not provided then all lines of the file are returned. If n provided, characters are read up to n but rounded up so that an entire line is returned. (Note: Ignored in the browser version). A list of strings, where each item represents a single line of the file. + Gives you a standard list you can manipulate with list operations immediately.- Unsafe for large files as it loads all lines into RAM simultaneously. When you specifically need the lines stored in a list structure for sorting, reversing, indexing, or checking the list length.

Note:

  • Adjust index for slicing because txt file lines are 1-indexed (conventionally), while Python lists/sequences are 0-indexed.
  • Use line.strip() on strings when reading from a file to remove any leading or trailing whitespace, including newline character before processing or printing(because print will automatically add a newline character ).

within with open("file_name.csv", mode) as file:

Returns a standard writer object. csv.DictWriter() writer = csv.DictWriter(file, fieldnames=["header_1", "header_2"]) Prepares a CSV file for structured writing mapped to specific keys. - file: An opened file object.- fieldnames: A list of strings representing column headers. Note: To add a column dynamically, we can use list concatenation + Prepares a CSV file for structured writing mapped to specific dictionary keys. writeheader() writer.writeheader() Only used with DictWriter. Writes a row with the column names specified in the fieldnames list to the file as the header row of the CSV. Note: If we just want to add a new column, simply append the value to the list/dict row then pass it to writer.writerow(row). Writes the fields to the corresponding columns and returns None.

docs.title: Comparison: Standard vs. Dictionary CSV Methods
docs.text:
Best practice: dictionary-based methods for writing defensive Python code.

Feature Standard Version (csv.reader / writer) Dictionary Version (csv.DictReader / DictWriter) Data Representation Handles rows as lists of strings. Handles rows as dictionaries. Access Method Numerical indices: row[0], row[1]. Header-name keys: row["header_1"], row["header_2"]. Robustness to Changes Fragile. If someone adds, swaps, or deletes columns, your index references will point to the wrong data and break your code. Highly Robust (Defensive). As long as the header names in the CSV remain consistent, the code will not break even if columns are added or swapped. CSV Headers Does not require or assume a header row. Requires a header row on the first line (or explicit fieldnames parameters when writing).

docs.title: Object-Oriented Programming (OOP)
docs.text:
Course source: CS50P Lecture 08

Object-Oriented Programming is a programming paradigm where you transition from writing code step-by-step (procedurally) to creating custom blueprints and data types (classes) .

docs.title: Core OOP Terminology
docs.text:
OOP is based on the concept of objects, defined by and associated with two things:

  • Attributes: data
  • Methods: functions

The most important feature: methods associated with the objects can access and modify the attributes of the objects via self. keyword.

Concept Purpose Syntax Details Behavior / Effect Class Acts as a custom blueprint or template to invent our own data type for modelling a real world entity and give it a name. class ClassName: ... Class name should be Capitalized by convention. The ... is a placeholder indicating the code will be finished later. Defines the attributes and behaviors that objects of this type will have. Objects / Instances Individual, concrete creation built using a class blueprint. An object is an instance of the class. instance = ClassName() Created using the class constructor syntax. Inherits all structure and methods defined in the class. Attributes (instance variables) Variables stored inside an object or class and operate on each instance. Within def: self.attribute = value Outside def:instance.attribute = value Accessed and set using dot notation. Standardizes the data that belongs to an instance. We can make it inmutable or mutable. Instance Methods Functions defined inside a class that dictates how each instance behave. Within def: self.method() Outside def:instance.method() Must take self as its first parameter to refer to the current object. Allows objects to perform custom actions and manipulate their own data. Class variables Shared variables for the entire class or across all the instances of the class, exist within class itself. Within def: class ClassName: class_variable = value

docs.title: Class Definition Template
docs.text:
encapsulate all the functionality of a class within the class definition. 

class ClassName(object_type):
     class_variable = value

     def __init__(self,argument_1, argument_2 = default_value,...): 
          self.attribute_1 = argument_1   # Note: no leading underscore (`_attribute`) in __init__ to make sure even this assignment goes through the setter. Without _, we are calling the getter and setter methods, not the actual attribute.  
          self.attribute_2 = argument_2   

     def __str__(self): 
          return f"{self.attribute}"

     def __add__(self, other):
          attribute_1 = self.attribute_1 + other.attribute_1
          attribute_2 = self.attribute_2 + other.attribute_2
          return ClassName(attribute_1, attribute_2)

     # getter and setter (similar for all the attributes)
     #  The `@property` (getter) must be defined before the `@<property>.setter`. 
     @property
     def attribute_1(self):
          return self._attribute_1

     @attribute_1.setter
     def attribute_1(self, argument):
          if argument not in [...]:    # validate attributes before assignments (and catch errors using try-except block when creating instances)
               raise SpecificErrorType("ErrorMessage")
          self._attribute_=1 = attribute_1

    @classmethod
    def get(cls, arguments):
        variable_1 = input("string prompt: ")
        variable_2 = input("string prompt: ")
        # create an new instance of the class
        return cls(variable_1, variable_2) 

def main():
    instance_name = ClassName.get()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Special Magic Methods __name__
docs.text:
If we define these Python special methods, Python would automatically call them.

Special Method Purpose Syntax Parameters Return Value __init__ The initialization method standardizes and initializes object attributes upon creation (The construct method is __new__ but we do not need to deal with it). def __init__(self, argument): self.attribute = argument - self: Refers to the current object being created. - Custom arguments passed during instantiation. Returns None automatically. Triggered by calling the class itself (e.g., constructor ClassName(args)). __str__ Defines how the object should represent itself as a text string for users. The return string is displayed automatically when the object is printed (e.g., print(instance)) def __str__(self): return f"{self.attribute}" - self: The current object. Must return a string. __repr__ Provides the “official” string representation that shows more info (type) (used in the Python shell, debugging, etc.) for developers __add__ Operator Overloading: Customizes how the + operator behaves between two objects. def __add__(self, other): return ... - self: The object on the left of +.- other: The object on the right of +. Returns a new object (or custom value) representing the sum of both objects.

docs.title: Getter and Setter - Define Properties using Decorators
docs.text:
To validate or restrict attributes before it is assigned to any values and avoid wrongly assignment, we define properties using function decorators (which begin with @)

Decorator Purpose Syntax Associated Parameter Note @property Defines a getter function to safely read an attribute. Note: The @property (getter) must be defined before the @<property>.setter. @propertydef attribute(self): return self._attribute self @property only and omitting the @<property>.setter decorator creates a read-only property. It will be called automatically whenver we access the attribute via .attribute Note the leading underscore (_attribute), which flags to programmers that this variable should not be modified directly. Python does not have the private/public keywords like C++, make sure not to touch the attributes with any leading underscore (_attribute) outside the class. @<attribute>.setter Defines a setter function to validate data before it is saved. @attribute.setterdef attribute(self, argument): if attribute not in [...]: raise ValueError() self._attribute = argument - self - argument: The new value being assigned. It will be called automatically whenver we access the attribute via .attribute = new_value @classmethod The function defined inside the class to add functionality to the class itself as a whole, not to each individual instance of that class. It does not have access to the object itself self but the class itself cls @classmethoddef class_method_name(cls, arguments): return cls(variables) # create an object of current class cls: Refers to the class itself, replacing the standard instance self. Can be called directly on the capitalized class name (e.g., ClassName.class_method_name()) without instantiating an object first. @staticmethod

docs.title: Built-In Type Checking (isinstance)
docs.text: Method Purpose Syntax Parameters Return Value isinstance() Checks whether an object is an instance of a specified class or data type (or tuple of types). if not isinstance(object, classinfo): raise ValueError("") - object: The variable/instance to inspect.- classinfo: A type (e.g., int, str, any class) or tuple of types (e.g., (int, float)). Returns True if the object matches the specified class/type; returns False otherwise.

docs.title: Inheritance
docs.text:
Allows a "child" class to inherit all the variables, attributes, and methods from its "parent" or ""gradparent" class. Eliminates redundant code when multiple classes share the same parameters and codes. We can even overwrite it if we want the child class to behave a bit differently than its parent class.

class Parent:
     def __init__(self, argument_1):
        if not argument_1:
            raise ValueError("Missing argument_1")
        self.argument_1 = argument_1

class Child(Parent):
     def __init__(self, argument_1, argument_2):
          super().__init__(argument_1)
          self.argument_2 = argument_2
Concept Purpose Syntax Example Explanatory Details super() Access the parent (or "super") class of the current class, letting the child call the parent methods. super().__init__(shared_arguments) Used inside a child's __init__ constructor to reuse the parent's initialization logic.

docs.title: Connecting to Exceptions Hierarchy
docs.text:
Python’s own exception system relies entirely on OOP inheritance. All exceptions are classes structured in a hierarchical parent-child tree: 

BaseException
 +-- KeyboardInterrupt
 +-- Exception
      +-- ArithmeticError
      |    +-- ZeroDivisionError
      +-- AssertionError
      +-- AttributeError
      +-- EOFError
      +-- ImportError
      |    +-- ModuleNotFoundError
      +-- LookupError
      |    +-- KeyError
      +-- NameError
      +-- SyntaxError
      |    +-- IndentationError
      +-- ValueError
 ...
This is why catching a parent exception like Exception also catches child exceptions like ValueError.

docs.title: Et Cetera
docs.text: Course source: CS50P Lecture 09

docs.title: Functional Programming
docs.text:
Functions themselves can be passed around as arguments/values.

taken a list and produced another list from it that contains either a subset of the items or a transformed version of each item.

  • When each item is transformed, we say that the operation is a mapping, or just a map of the original list.
  • When some items are omitted, we call it a filter.
Method Purpose Syntax Parameters Return Value Example map() (not preferred) Applies a specified function to every element across a sequence. map(transform_function, iterable) - transform_function: The function to apply to each element to transform each element to a new element. - iterable: One or more iterable objects (list, tuple, etc.) whose elements will be processed. A map iterator containing the transformed items. words = ["this", "is", "cs50"]uppercased = map(str.upper, words) filter()(not preferred) Extracts a subset of a sequence for which a conditional function returns True. filter(filter_function, iterable) - filter_function: A function or lambda expression returning boolean True/False for each item. - iterable: The target sequence to filter. A filter iterator containing only the matching items. students = [{"name": "Harry", "house": "Gryffindor"}, ...]gryffindors = filter(lambda s: s["house"] == "Gryffindor", students)

Note that:

  • Only pass the function name without (), because we do not call the functions there; the functions will be called for each items later.
  • Return a iterator -> we need to cast it to list , e.g., list(map()) or list(filter())

docs.title: List Comprehension
docs.text:
a concise way to create new lists from other lists in one elegant one-liner, optionally combine map and filter operation together. 

my_list = [transform_expression for item in iterable if filter_condition]

  • The if clause (optional) is for a filter operation.
  • The transformer_expression is for mapping operation.
When to use Code syntax init 2D matrix (m rows and n columns) [[default_value] * n for _ in range(m)]

docs.title: Dictionary Comprehension
docs.text:
(similar to List comprehension) a concise way to create a new dictionary from other lists, optionally combine map and filter operation together. 

my_dict = {key_expression : value_expression for item in iterable if filter_condition}

  • The if clause (optional) is for a filter operation.
  • The key_expression and value_expressionis are for mapping operation.
  • e.g., counts = {word : words.count(word) for word in words}

docs.title: Generators
docs.text: We can define a function as generators whereby it can still generate a massive amount of data by returning one item at a time instead of storing everything in memory, preventing memory exhaustion or crashing.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
def generator_name():
    for i in range(n):
        yield object

my_generator = generator_name()
next(my_generator)
# do something else
next(my_generator)
Details: To create the next successive, we can simply call next() on the generator object, and it will yield the next iteration. After yield is called, everything in the state of the generator function freezes, and the value is returned. When the generator is called again with next(), it picks back up right where it stopped at yield from before.

docs.title: Python Generators vs. Functions
docs.text: Feature Function Generator When to use Standard tasks where the data fits in memory and can be computed and returned all at once. Dealing with very large collections of data that we cannot store in memory all at once (which leads to program hanging or crush). Functionalities Return a value and exiting the this function. Pause the process, save its state for next time, [optionally do other things] and continue Biggest difference return keyword: return all at once yield keyword: return one item at a time while the for loop keeps working. (return an iterator so we can use for loop to iterate over the generated value one at a time)

docs.title: Flattened Generator Expression
docs.text:
Feature Description What It Is A generator expression that iterates through nested 2D structures (e.g., list of lists for grid, matrix, game board) and yields items as a single 1D stream. Why Use It Processes elements lazily (one by one) to save memory instead of building a full intermediate list in RAM. Common Use Case Feeding flattened elements directly into aggregator functions (e.g., Counter(), sum(), set(), "".join()). 
from collections import Counter 
# 2D Grid / Board 
board = [
    ["🍪", "🍪", "🐍"], ["🐍", "🍪", "🍪"],
]   

# using a Flattened Generator Expression (Memory Efficient): 
counts = Counter(char for row in board for char in row) 

print(counts) # Output: Counter({'🍪': 4, '🐍': 2}) 


# The exact same behavior written with a explicit generator function: 
def stream_board(grid): 
    for row in grid: 
        for char in row: 
            yield char 

counts = Counter(stream_board(board))

docs.title: Generator Expression vs. List Comprehension for Flattening
docs.text: Approach Syntax Example Memory Overhead Execution Behavior Generator Expression (char for row in board for char in row) Low \(O(1)\) RAM Generates and yields items lazily one at a time on demand. Nested yield Loop for row in board: for char in row: yield char Low \(O(1)\) RAM Standard multi-line function logic equivalent to the generator expression. List Comprehension [char for row in board for char in row] High \(O(N)\) RAM Allocates and constructs the full flattened list in memory immediatelys.

docs.title: build in methods
docs.text: Method Purpose Syntax Parameters Return Value Complexities Examples print() Outputs one or more objects to the console or another text stream. Useful for displaying values, debugging, and writing formatted text. print(*objects, sep=' ', end='\n', file=None, flush=False) -*objects: * means the method can take multiple arguments, i.e., arbitrary number of objects to print. Here we can also take a big argument using + to concatenate strings. - sep (optional): Seperator inserted between objects automatically. Default: blank space ' '. - end (optional): String appended for line ending. Default: new line '\n'. - file (optional): A file-like object with a write() method. Default: standard output. - flush (optional): If True, forcibly flushes the stream. Default: False. Return None. Time: O(n), Space: O(1) input() Reads a line of text from standard input, usually entered by the user, and optionally displays a prompt before reading. input([prompt]) prompt (optional): A string displayed to the user before input is read. Default: no prompt. Return the user input as a string, excluding the trailing newline. Note: Use int() or float() to convert data type if the input is a number and will be used in calculation. Time: O(n), Space: O(n) input_variable_name = input("text prompt")

docs.title: Unpacking
docs.text: Concept Description Example Details Unpacking List(*) Unpacks elements of a list or tuple into positional arguments when calling a function. function(*my_list) Passes each element of the sequence as an individual argument. Note that the list/tuple/dict element size should be the same as the number of arguments of the function, otherwise, it will raise TypeError Unpacking Dictionary(**) Unpacks key-value pairs of a dictionary into named keyword arguments. my_dict = {"key__1": value_1, "key__2": value_2}function(**my_dict) Matches dictionary keys to function parameter, and pass the values, seperate conceptually with equal signs function(my_dict[key_1], my_dict[key_2])

docs.title: Placeholder *args and **kwargs
docs.text:
To tell our functions to expect a presently unknown variadic number of positional arguments / keyword arguments. *args and **kwargs can be named differently, e.g., *objects

Concept Description Syntax *args Parameter (can be called with different names) Could take an arbitrary number of positional arguments(from left to right) into a tuple, i.e., args = (value_1, value_2, value_3) def f(*args): f(value_1, value_2, value_3) **kwargs Parameter Could take an arbitrary number of keyword arguments (can be called optionally and individually by its own name) into a dictionary, i.e., kwargs = {arg_1 : value_1, arg_2 : value_2, arg_3 : value_3} def f(**kwargs): f(arg_1 = value_1, arg_2 = value_2, arg_3 = value_3)

docs.title: global vs. Local Variables
docs.text:
Note: OOP classes are preferred over global variables.

The rule of thumb: Use global variables sparingly.

Feature Local Variable Global Variable Where defined Inside a function Outside all functions (at the top) Scope (Access) Only inside that function Anywhere in the module Lifetime Exists only while function runs Exists for the entire program execution Modification Assign directly var = 10 Requires global keyword to tell each function that var does not refer to a local variable: instead, it refers to the global variable we originally placed at the top of our code. global var var = 10

Note: Do not have a local variable that has the same name as any global variable.

docs.title: Constant Variable
docs.text:
Constant variable are intended to remain unchangeable throughout program execution, typically denoted by all capital variable names and are placed at the top of our code. Note: Python does not enforce constant immutability like other languages, we can only name it in ALL_CAPS to indicate "Do not change it", i.e., Python actually has no mechanism to prevent us from changing that value.

Class constants are defined within class but outside of any particular class method and can be accessed via ClassName.CONSTANT

docs.title: Lambda Function
docs.text:
Feature Regular Function Lambda Function (alternative way for creating a simple function) When to use General purpose, especially when for complex expressions and reusable functions When an anonymous simple, temporary function is needed immediately, not intended to be reused multiple times, such as when using inline operations, as arguments to higher-order functions (map, filter, sorted) Syntax def fn_name(arguments): block of code return expression_or_var lambda arguments: expression Syntax details Starts with def keyword followed by the function name, arguments, and a block of code for multiple expressions, optionally explicit return statement. Starts with lambda keyword followed by parameters, a colon, and a single expression.* arguments: A comma-separated list of parameters* expression: A single expression that is evaluated and returned automatically. Example def add(x, y): return x + y lambda x, y: x + y Scope of Variables Can define local variables for use within the function. Cannot define new variables; can only use function arguments and existing variables.

Figure: Regular Function vs Lambda Function

docs.title: Check Type Hints Using mypy
docs.text:
In other programming languages, one expresses explicitly what variable type one wants to use, however, Python does not require the explicit declaration of types. Nevertheless, it’s good practice to ensure all of your variables are of the right type.

pip install mypymypy file_name.py

Concept Purpose Syntax + Type Hints Annotates the expected types for arguments, variable and return values for static analysis. def function(argument: arg_type) -> return_type: variable: var_type = value return return_var Improves code readability and allows type checkers to catch errors before runtime.

docs.title: Docstrings
docs.text:
Standardized multiline comments placed inside functions to document function behavior / features within triple quotes """.

Document fields (:param, :return, etc.) can be parsed by tools such as Sphinx, to parse docstrings and automatically create documentation in the form of web pages and PDF files such that you can publish and share with others. 

    def function_name(argument: arg_type) -> return_type:
        """
        One-sentence explanation of the function.

        :param argument: description
        type argument: arg_type
        :raise ErrorType: If statement 
        :return: description
        rtype: return_type
        """
We could also include sample input and sample output in the docstrings.

docs.title: Characteristics & Definition
docs.text:
data structure that allows us to store associated info - associate keys with values.

Feature Description Sequence unordered, mutable (changeable) collection of key-value pairs Mutable (changeable) We can modify, add, or remove items after creation Key is unique cannot have two same keys Element Types keys and values can contain elements of same types and even different types (e.g., strings, integers) Creation Syntax enclosed by curly braces {} with key-value pairs key: value separated by commas , When to Use Dictionary - When we want to return multiple values, we can pack them into a dictionary - When the value should be able to be changed - When we store more fields, it is easier to index via keys instead of indices.
  • If value == None : Indicates no data is assigned to that key.
  • Clean formatting: Separate into multiple lines 
    dict = {
    key_1: value_1, 
    key_2: value_2, 
    ... , 
    key_n : value_n
}

docs.text:
accessing keys (not via position index)

Action Syntax / Example Detail Access Value - dict[key] - dict.get(key, default_value) Retrieves the value for the key. - dict[key] might get key error if key is not existing - dict.get() (preferred) method won't get key error Reassign dict[key] = new_value changing values by accessing keys (not via position index) and resigning a new value adding new key and new value dict[new_key] = new_value resigning a value to a new key

docs.text: Method Purpose Syntax Parameters Return Value Complexities Example get() Retrieve value for the key safely - never raises KeyError. d.get(key, default = None) - key - default (optional) Return the value for key if key is in the dictionary, otherwise default if key is missing \(O(1)\) d.get("apple", 0) keys() Return a new view of all keys in the dictionary. d.keys() None Return a new view of the dictionary’s keys. \(O(1)\) d.keys() values() Return a view of all values in the dictionary. Note: An equality comparison between one dict.values() view and another will always return False. This also applies when comparing dict.values() to itself. d.values() None Return a new view of the dictionary’s values. \(O(1)\) d.values() == d.values() -> False items() Return key-value pairs for iteration. d.items() None Return a new view of the dictionary’s items, i.e., (key, value) pairs \(O(1)\) for k, v in d.items(): pop() Remove key and return its value. d.pop(key, default) key, default (optional) Value or default \(O(1)\) d.pop("milk") popitem() Remove/return last inserted key-value pair. d.popitem() None (key, value) pair \(O(1)\) k, v = d.popitem() update() Update dict with another dict or iterable. d.update(other) Another dict/iterable None \(O(len(other))\) d.update({"bread": 1}) setdefault() Get value if key exists, else set/return default. d.setdefault(k, def) key, default Value \(O(1)\) d.setdefault("eggs", 1) clear() Remove all items from the dictionary. d.clear() None None \(O(1)\) d.clear() copy() Create a shallow copy of the dictionary. d.copy() None New dict \(O(n)\) new_d = d.copy()

docs.text:
Requires: from collections import defaultdict, Counter

Method Purpose Syntax Parameters Return Value Complexities Example defaultdict() Create dict with default factory for missing keys. defaultdict(factory) factory (e.g., int) defaultdict object \(O(1)\) d = defaultdict(int) Counter() Count hashable elements in an iterable. Counter(iterable) iterable or mapping Counter object \(O(n)\) c = Counter(list) most_common() Return k most frequent elements. c.most_common(k) k (optional) List of (elem, count) \(O(n \log k)\) c.most_common(1)

docs.title: Iterables
docs.text:
Anything you can loop over with a for loop is an iterable.

  • ordered sequences (string, list, tuple): support indexing and slicing.
  • unordered collections (dictionary, set): support indexing but not slicing.

docs.title: Slicing for Ordered Sequences
docs.text:
a universal technique in Python used to extract parts of ordered sequences (string, list, tuple).

Syntax Meaning Note data[start: stop: step] - : separate start, stop, and step - Inclusive Start, Exclusive Stop, i.e., [start, stop) - optional: Omitting start means "from beginning" - optional: Omitting stop means "to end" Negative indices means count from the end -1 means the last element -2 means the last 2nd element step determine selection intervals Negative step reverses order

docs.title: Slicing cheat sheet
docs.text:
Operation Syntax Meaning Example ("Python") Output Complexities Basic Slicing data[start:stop] Extract elements from start to stop-1. "Python"[1:4] "yth" \(O(k)\) where \(k = \text{stop} - \text{start}\) Omitting start data[:stop] start from the beginning up to stop-1. "Python"[:4] "Pyth" \(O(k)\) Omitting stop data[start:] From start to the end. "Python"[2:] "thon" \(O(k)\) Using step data[start:stop:step] Extract with step intervals. Python"[::2] "Pto" \(O(k)\) Full Slice data[:] Return the entire sequence. "Python"[:] "Python" \(O(n)\) Negative Indexing data[-start:-stop] Count from the end (-1 is the last element). "Python"[-5:-2] "yth" \(O(k)\) Reverse a Sequence data[::-1] Reverse the sequence. Python"[::-1] "nohtyP" \(O(n)\) Skipping Elements data[::k] Select every k-th element. "Python"[::3] "Ph" \(O(n/k)\) Negative Step data[start:stop: -step] Pick elements in reverse order. "Python"[4:1:-1] "oht" \(O(k)\)

Note: slicing create new lists -> space O(n)

docs.title: Build-in Methods for General Iterables
docs.text: Method Purpose Scope Syntax Parameters Return Value Complexities sorted() Build a new sorted list from any iterable. Uses Timsort. any iterable sorted(iterable, key=None, reverse=False) - iterable: Any iterable object. - key (Optional): Same as list.sort(). A function or callable taking one argument as sorting criteria. Note: just function name without(). Default: lexicographical order for nested lists (i.e., first sort by x[0], if x[0] is the same, further sorts by x[1]). • Multi-level of sorting: from operator import itemgetter, attrgetter key = itemgetter(obj_idx_1, obj_idx_2) or key = attrgetter(obj_attr_1, obj_attr_2) • use partial() to reduce arugments: from functools import partial key=partial(multi_argument_func) - reverse (Optional): Same as list.sort(). Boolean flag for order. Default: ascending (False); descending (True). New sorted list Time: \(O(n \log n)\)Space: \(O(n)\) zip() Combine multiple iterables element-wise into tuples.Additional Tricks:• Unzip: var1, var2 = zip(*var)• Chunking a list into equal size n: zip(*[iter(s)] * n, strict=True) any iterable zip(*iterables, strict=False) - *iterables: Two or more any iterable inputs. - strict (Optional): Boolean flag for equal length. If True, forces equal length check. Default False (stops when the shortest iterable is exhausted, ignore the remaining items in the longer iterables). If iterables must to be of equal length, set strict=True A iterator of tuples, one tuple per index position (a lazy iterator, so no actual tuples are created until you iterate or convert it using list(), set(), etc.) Time: \(O(n)\)Space: \(O(1)\) (lazy, unless cast) .index() Return the index of the first occurrence of value in sequence. any sequence (list, string, tuple) sequence.index(value[, start[, stop]]) - value: value to find -start/end: (optional) search range (efficient searching of subsections without copying any data.) Caution: Not all sequence types support passing the start and stop arguments. int (index of match); raises ValueError if not found \(O(n)\)

docs.title: Characteristics & Definition
docs.text:
Lists are a data type used to store a collection of items in a specific order.

Feature Description Sequence finite, ordered, mutable sequence of elements Mutable (changeable) We can modify, add, or remove items after creation Element Types List can contain elements of same types and even different types (e.g., strings, integers, or even dictionaries, lists.) Creation Syntax enclosed by square brackets [] with elements separated by commas list = [elem_1, elem_2, ..., elem_n]. When to Use List - When we want to return multiple values, we can pack them into a list - When the value should be able to be changed

docs.title: Creation
docs.text: Operation Syntax Description Complexity Create a list with \(n\) same objects list = [value] * n Creates a list of length n. This is fine for immutable objects (e.g. int, str). \(O(n)\) Create a list with \(n\) distinct mutable objects list = [[] for _ in range(n)] Use list comprehension for distinct sub-lists or other mutable objects. [[]] * n would create the same sub-list referenced \(n\) times. \(O(n)\)

docs.title: Accessing & Modifying Elements
docs.text:
Python list uses 0-based indexing, meaning the first item is at position 0.

Action Detail Syntax Complexity Access Retrieve the value at the \(i\)-th position list[i] \(O(1)\) Reassign Change a value by accessing value via its position index and assigning a new value. list[i] = new_value \(O(1)\) Check if an item is in list In the worst case: Python checks each element. For membership tests, consider using a set if we need repeated lookups. if item in lst: \(O(n)\)

docs.title: General Operations (Polymorphic Tools)
docs.text:
These tools work on multiple data types, including strings, lists, and more.

Tool Purpose Syntax Parameters Return Value Notes Complexity len() Return the number of items/characters in an object. len(obj) An iterable (list, string, etc.) int Essential for dynamic loops like range(len(list)). + operator Concatenate two sequences of the same type. s1 + s2 Two sequences (2 lists or 2 strings) New sequence Creates a new object; does not modify the originals in-place. \(O(len(a) + len(b))\) * operator Repeat a sequence a specified number of times. s * n A sequence and an int New sequence

docs.title: List build-in methods
docs.text: Method Purpose Syntax Parameters Return Value Complexity Example .append() Add an item to the end of the list. list.append(value) value: Any object None Amortized \(O(1)\) lst = [1, 2, 3] lst.append([4, 5]) output: [1, 2, 3, [4, 5]] .extend() Unpack an iterable and adds all its items to the end of list. list.extend(iterable) iterable: the iterable (e.g., list/tuple, string) None \(O(k)\) where \(k\) is length of the iterable l1 = [1, 2, 3]l2 = [4, 5] l1.extend(l2) output: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] .insert() Insert an item at a specific index. list.insert(index, value) - index: Position where the element will be inserted. - value: Item to be added to the list. None \(O(n)\) a = [1, 2, 5] a.insert(2, [3, 4]) output: [1, 2, [3, 4], 5] .remove() Remove the first occurrence of a specific value. It raises a ValueError if there is no such item. list.remove(value) value: Value to find None \(O(n)\) lst = [5, 10, 5, 15, 5]lst.remove(5) output: [10, 5, 15, 5] .pop() Remove the item at given index \(i\)(default is last) and return it. It raises an IndexError if the list is empty or the index is outside the list range. list.pop(index=-1) index: (Optional) Position of the element to remove. The removed item - \(O(1)\) (at the end)- \(O(n)\) (random index) lst = ["red", "blue", "green", "yellow"]val = lst.pop(1) output: ['red', 'green', 'yellow'] .clear() Remove all items from the list. list.clear() None None \(O(n)\) l.clear() # results in [] .reverse() Reverses the elements of the list in-place. list.reverse() None None \(O(n)\) lst = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]lst.reverse() output[5, 4, 3, 2, 1] list.sort() Sort list in-place. Only defined for lists. Uses Timsort. s list.sort(key=None, reverse=False) - key (Optional): A function or callable taking one argument as sorting criteria. Note: just function name without(). Default: lexicographical order for nested lists (i.e., first sort by x[0], if x[0] is the same, further sorts by x[1]). • Multi-level of sorting: from operator import itemgetter, attrgetter key = itemgetter(obj_idx_1, obj_idx_2) or key = attrgetter(obj_attr_1, obj_attr_2) • use partial() to reduce arugments: from functools import partial key=partial(multi_argument_func) - reverse (Optional): : Boolean flag for order. Default: ascending (False); descending (True). Return None (modifies list in place) Time: \(O(n \log n)\)Space: \(O(n)\) .count() Return the number of times a value appears. list.count(x) x: Value int \(O(n)\) num = l.count("Gryffindor")

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text: Category Items Examples Data Types int (integers), float (decimal/real numbers), complex(a,b) (complex number a+bi). Type Casting convert data types e.g., after getting input from command line via input(), remember to use int(variable) or float(variable) to convert data types from string to numbers. Readable Big Numbers use underscores _ as the seperator n = 100_000_000

docs.title: Python Arithmetic Operators
docs.text: Method Purpose Syntax Parameters Return Value Complexities Example + Adds two numbers. x + y x, y: numeric values Sum of x and y Time: O(1)Space: O(1) 3 + 2 -> 5 - Subtracts the second number from the first. x - y x, y: numeric values Difference of x and y Time: O(1)Space: O(1) 5 - 2 -> 3 * Multiplies two numbers. x * y x, y: numeric values Product of x and y Time: O(1)Space: O(1) 4 * 3 -> 12 / Divides the first number by the second. It is essential for determining Parity (whether a number is even or odd) x % y x, y: numeric values, y != 0 Remainder of x divided by y Time: O(1)Space: O(1) 5 % 2 -> 1 - even: n % 2 == 0 - odd: n % 2 != 0 ** Exponent: Raises the first number to the power of the second. x ** y x: base valuey: exponent x raised to the power y Depends on operand size 2 ** 3 -> 8

docs.text: Method Purpose Syntax Parameters Return Value Complexities Example abs() Return the absolute value of a number. abs(x) x: integer, float, or another numeric object Absolute value of x Time: O(1)Space: O(1) abs(-7) -> 7 int() Converts a number or numeric string to an integer. For floats, it truncates toward 0. int(x, base=10) - x: number, string, bytes, or bytearray - base (optional): base of the input when x is a string-like value Integer value Time: O(n) for string input; O(1) for numeric inputSpace: O(1) int("42") -> 42int(3.9) -> 3 float() Converts a number or numeric string to a floating-point number. float(x) x: number or string Floating-point value Time: O(n) for string input; optionally computes modulo efficiently. pow(base, exp[, mod]) - base: base value - exp: exponent - mod (optional): modulus base ** exp, or modular exponentiation result Depends on numeric type and operand size pow(2, 5) -> 32pow(2, 5, 3) -> 2 divmod() Return the quotient and remainder together. divmod(a, b) a: dividendb: divisor Tuple (quotient, remainder) Time: O(1)Space: O(1) divmod(17, 5) -> (3, 2) max() Return the largest item in an iterable or the largest of multiple arguments. max(iterable, *[, key, default])max(arg1, arg2, *args, key=None) iterable: iterable to inspectarg1, arg2, ...: values to comparekey (optional): function for comparison keydefault (optional): fallback for empty iterable Largest item Time: O(n)Space: O(1) max([3, 1, 9]) -> 9 min() Return the smallest item in an iterable or the smallest of multiple arguments. min(iterable, *[, key, default])min(arg1, arg2, *args, key=None) iterable: iterable to inspectarg1, arg2, ...: values to comparekey (optional): function for comparison keydefault (optional): fallback for empty iterable Smallest item Time: O(n)Space: O(1) min([3, 1, 9]) -> 1 sum() Adds items of an iterable from left to right, starting from an optional initial value. sum(iterable[, start]) iterable: iterable of numbersstart (optional): initial value, default 0 Total sum Time: O(n)Space: O(1) sum([1, 2, 3]) -> 6

docs.title: Characteristics & Definition
docs.text:
data structure for a collection of values that allows us to eliminate duplicates.

Feature Description Container unordered, mutable (changeable) collection of values Mutable (changeable) We can modify, add, or remove items after creation Unique No duplicates Element Types Creation Syntax my_set= set() When to Use Set - When we want to make sure there is no duplicates - When the value should be able to be changed

docs.title: String Operator Overloading
docs.text: Syntax Application Example Concatenation (+) chain strings together. str1 + str2 *multiplicaton () repeat strings n times print(str_variable * n)

docs.title: Output Formatting (f-strings)
docs.text:
prefixing a string with f, expressions inside {} are evaluated at runtime, making it simple to embed variable values and expressions directly within string literals.

f"{value:format}"

Parts Meaning value The variable or expression we want to print. colon : The separator that tells Python everything after this is a formatting instruction. format Special codes that tell Python how to display that value.

docs.title: f-strings Patterns Cheat Sheet
docs.text: Feature Meaning Syntax Examples Interpolation Inject variables into strings. f"other_text, {variable_name or expression}" Thousands Formate large number variable num with commas , f"{num:,}" print(f"{num:,}") 1000000 -> 1,000,000 Precision round the output variable num to the nearest n decimal points. Here n is a number and it could not be 0. f"{num:.nf}" print(f"{num:.2f}") 3.1415926 -> 3.14 Percentage automatically convert float output variable num to percentage, add %sign and keep the nearest n decimal points. f"{num:.n%}" f"{num:.0%}" 0.75 -> "75%" Padding Pad or fill a string with the specified padding character pad_char to a specific total width total_width: - Center the string and pad both sides using ^: f"{str:{pad_char}^total_width}" - Padding from the right using <: f"{str:{pad_char}<total_width}" - Padding from the" left using >: f"{str:{pad_char}>total_width}" - zero-padding for numbers: f"{num:0total_width}" - f"{str:{pad_char}^{width}}" string "GFG" pad with character "-" becomes "----GFG-----" - zero-padding: f"{num:02}" "9" becomes "09"

docs.title: String build-in methods
docs.text: Method Purpose Syntax Parameters Return Value Complexities Example len() Return the length of the string. len(str) str: The input string. Return an integer representing the number of characters in the string. .strip() Stripe oﬀ (Removes) any leading and trailing specified characters (default: whitespace). str.strip([chars]) chars (optional): specified characters to remove. Return a new string with characters removed from both ends. str_variable_name = str_variable_name.strip() .lstrip() Remove leading (left) whitespace or specified characters. Note: not remove characters in between str.lstrip([chars]) Same as strip(). Return a new string with leading characters removed. .rstrip() Remove trailing (right) whitespace or specified characters. Note: not remove characters in between str.rstrip([chars]) Same as strip(). Return a new string with trailing characters removed. .capitalize() Capitalize the first character of the string. str.capitalize() None Return a new string with only the first letter capitalized. str_variable_name = str_variable_name.capitalize() .title() Capitalize the first letter of each word. str.title() None Return a new string with each word's first letter capitalized. str_variable_name = str_variable_name.title() .lower() Convert all characters in a string to lowercase. str.lower() None Return a copy of the string with all the cased characters converted to lowercase. str_variable_name = str_variable_name.lower() .upper() Convert all characters in a string to uppercase. str.upper() None Return a copy of the string with all the cased characters converted to uppercase. str_variable_name = str_variable_name.upper() .split() Split a string into a list of substrings based on a specified delimiter. Splitting an empty string with a specified separator Return ['']. str.split(sep=None, maxsplit=-1) - sep (optional): separator delimiter - string or char, such as ','. Default: whitespace. > If sep is not specified or is None, runs of consecutive whitespace are regarded as a single separator, and the result will contain no empty strings at the start or end if the string has leading or trailing whitespace. Consequently, splitting an empty string or a string consisting of just whitespace with a None separator Return []. In addition, if maxsplit==0, only leading runs of consecutive whitespace are considered. > If sep is given, consecutive delimiters are deemed to delimit empty strings. -maxsplit (optional): Maximum number of splits. Default: -1 means no limit (all possible splits are made). Return a list of substrings. If failed, raise ValueError: not enough values to unpack Time: O(n), Space: O(n) str_variable_name_1, str_variable_name_2, ... str_variable_name_n = str_variable_name.split() '1,2,,3,'.split(',') ['1', '2', '', '3', ''] ' 1 2 3 '.split() ['1', '2', '3'] "".split(None, 0) [] " ".split(None, 0) [] " foo ".split(maxsplit=0)['foo '] .rsplit() Behave like split(), except for splitting from the right. str.rsplit(sep=None, maxsplit=-1) - sep (optional): separator delimiter - string or char, such as ','. Default: whitespace. -maxsplit (optional): at most maxsplit splits are done, the rightmost ones. Default: -1 means no limit (all possible splits are made). Return a list of substrings. Time: O(n), Space: O(n) .join() Join elements of an iterable into a single string with a specified delimiter placed between each element. sep.join(iterable) - sep: separator delimiter. -iterable: A sequence of strings (e.g., list, tuple, dict etc) to join together. When using it with a dict, it will only join the keys, not the values. Return a concatenated string. Time: O(n), Space: O(n) .replace() Replace all occurrences of an old substring by a new substring. docs.title: Logical Deduction
docs.text:
An inference rule is a rule for combining true propositions to form other true propositions. We can quickly verify an inference rule using truth table.

Rule Meaning \(((P \implies Q) \space \text{AND} \space P) \implies Q\) If \(P\) implies \(Q\), and \(P\) is true, then \(Q\) must be true. \(((P \implies Q) \space \text{AND} \space \text{NOT}\space Q) \implies \text{NOT} \space P\) If \(P\) would imply \(Q\), but \(Q\) is false, then \(P\) must be false. \(((P \implies Q) \space\text{AND}\space (Q \implies R)) \implies (P \implies R)\) If \(P\) would imply \(Q\), and \(Q\) would imply \(R\), then \(P\) must implie \(R\). \(((\text{NOT} \space P) \implies \text{FALSE}) \implies P\) If assume Not \(P\) leads to a contradiction, then \(P\) must be true.

Example: \(P \implies Q\): If it rains, the ground gets wet.

When write a proof:

  • Each step in a proof should be clear and logical.
  • You should state which previously proved propositions are being used.
  • Please do not make wild leaps of faith.
  • Please do not use “Proof by Intimidation” (obvious, Clearly etc)
  • But we are not picky about which inference rules you use, and there is certainly no need to cite an inference rule at every step.

docs.title: Proof Outlining
docs.text:
This outlining step can often be started nearly mechanically, based on the form of the theorem being proved and the chosen proof techniques.

  • Choosing a proof method can lead to immediate and noticeable progress on constructing the proof.
  • Break down a proof into smaller tasks precisely,and tackle these tasks one at a time.
  • Consider multiple possible approaches to a problem before deciding which one(s) to pursue.

A common proof-writing mistake is to dive into how to prove something, while not realizing that you’re trying to prove the wrong thing! Spending a bit of time identifying what needs to be proved, likely using our common proof techniques, will ensure that your “how to prove”-energy is directed at the correct targets.

docs.text: Let \(P(n)\) be a predicate (Induction Hypothesis), defned for \(n \in \mathbb{N}\). If \(P(0)\) and \(\forall n \geq 0.[P(n) \implies P(n+1)]\), then \(\forall n \geq 0. P(n)\)

docs.title: Note: strengthen the inductive hypothesis
docs.text:
Often (but not always!) this \(P(n)\) will be the predicate we initially set out to prove, however sometimes we might need to strengthen the inductive hypothesis using a stronger \(Q(n)\) instead of original \(P(n)\).

Example: \(P(n)\) is the predicate "it is possible to use non-overlapping L-trominoes to cover a \(2^n\) by \(2^n\) square grid, except for one of the center-most squares". \(Q(n)\) is the stronger hypothesis "it is possible to use non-overlapping L-trominoes to cover a \(2^n\) by \(2^n\) square” except for any one square".

Figure: Example of strengthen the inductive hypothesis: Algorithm divide and conquer - Cut the grid into divide and conquerfour quadrants and put a L-trominoes in the middle.

docs.title: Strong Induction
docs.text:
Suppose \(P(n)\) is a predicate with n a natural-number variable. Suppose that

  1. \(P(0)\) is true.
  2. \(\forall n \in \mathbb{N}\), it holds that \(IH(n) = P(0) \land P(1) \land . . . P(n) \implies P(n + 1)\).

Then it holds that \(\forall n \in \mathbb{N}, P(n)\)

Note: Strong induction is in fact completely equivalent to regular induction, and the strong induction theorem can easily be proven from the Axiom of Induction by using the regular induction Axioms for the new induction hypothesis \(IH(n)\).

Figure: Strong Induction Intuition - not only assume \(P(0)\) but also assume all the \(P(i)\) is true, where \(i \in \mathbb{N}, i < n\)

docs.title: State Machines
docs.text:
Course source: 6.1200J Lecture 04

Aspects Explanation Note Definition a collection of states \(Q\), a specified initial state \(q_0 \in Q\), and a set of allowed transitions \(T\), for each state: a (possibly empty) list of possible transitions to other states \(q \to r\). If a state has multiple possible transitions, we say the state machine is non-deterministic; otherwise, it is deterministic. An execution of a state machine a (in)finite sequence of states, starting from the initial state, that follows the transition rules, i.e., \(q_0 \to q_1 \to q_2 \to \cdots (\to q_n)\), where each \(q_i \to q_{i+1} \in T\)

docs.title: Reachability and invariants
docs.text:
Terms/Features Explanation Note Reachability A state \(r\) is reachable if there is some execution that reaches that state \(q_0 \to \cdots \to r\) If there is no possible execution, the state is unreachable Predicate \(P(q)\) is true or false depending on state \(q \in Q\) We could think about it as a function from a set of states \(Q\) to boolean values \(\{\text{true}, \text{false}\}\) Preserved Predicate a predicate \(P(\cdot)\) defined on states, such that the truth of \(P(\cdot)\) is preserved along transitions, i.e., if \(P(q)\) is true for a state \(q\), and there exists a transition \(q \to r \in T\) from \(q\) to \(r\), then \(P(r)\) is true as well. i.e., \(\forall q \to r \in T,\; P(q) \to P(r)\) Invariant a property \(P(q)\) that is true for all reachable states. Proof by Invariant Principle. Steps:1. Show \(P(q_0)\) is true 2. Show \(P(q)\) is preserved. Consider any \(q \to r \in T\), assume \(P(q)\) is true, want to show \(P(r)\) is true Theorem - The Invariant Principle (generalization of the induction axioms, can be proved by strong induction): Suppose \(P(\cdot)\) is true for the initial state \(q_0\), i.e., \(P(q_0)\) is true and is a preserved predicate, i.e., \(\forall q \to r \in T,\; P(q) \to P(r)\). Then \(P(\cdot)\) is an invariant. Corollary (following the theorem): If \(P(r)\) is false and \(P(\cdot)\) is an invariant, then state \(r\) is unreachable

Example: 8 puzzle

  • \(P(q)\) = the number of inverted pairs in state \(q\) is odd
  • \(P(q)\) is preserved because
    • Horizontal moves: The order does not change, so P(r) is true
    • Vertical moves: Consider the sequence \(i, j, k, *\). Moving \(i\) downwards—swapping \(i \leftrightarrow *\)—is equivalent to swapping \(i \leftrightarrow j\) and then \(i \leftrightarrow k\) (two adjacent swaps in reading order). Each swap changes the number of inverted pairs by either \(+1\) or \(-1\). Therefore, two adjacent swaps change the number of inverted pairs by \((\pm 1) + (\pm 1) = \text{even}\). When \(P(q)\) is true, the number of inverted pairs is odd; after this operation, it is still odd, so \(P(r)\) remains true.
  • Then use invariant principle and Corollary to prove states are reachable or unreachable

docs.title: Termination
docs.text:
Terms/Features Explanation Note final state state \(q\) with no possible transitions. no \(q \to r \in T\) terminate definition if there are no infinite executions. Intuitively, if we try to run the state machine, then no matter what choices we make for each transition, we end up at a final state. It means the algorithm will not run forever. correct if the state machine terminates and partially correct partially correct means if the state machine terminates then it gives correct answer derived variable (aka potential function) a function \(X(q)\) mapping states \(Q\) to real numbers \(\mathbb{R}\), i.e., for each state \(q \in Q\), value \(X(q) \in \mathbb{R}\) Analog to state predicates: state predicates \(P(q)\) map state \(Q\) to boolean values \(\{\text{true}, \text{false}\}\) A derived variable \(X(q)\) is strictly decreasing if, for any transition \(\forall q \to r \in T\), \(X(q) < X(r)\). It is weakly decreasing if \(X(q) \le X(r)\). Termination Theorem Suppose \(X(q)\) is a derived variable with natural number (non-negative integer) values that is strictly decreasing. Then we are guaranteed the state machine terminates. i.e., satisfying 1. \(X(q) \in \mathbb{N}, \forall q \in Q\) 2. \(X(q)\) is strictly decreasing It can be proved by induction. The idea is that all executions have length \(\le X(q_0)\)

Example - simple sort

  • Algorithm: while \(\exists i,\; a_i > a_{i+1}\), swap \(a_i \leftrightarrow a_{i+1}\).
  • \(X(q)\) is the number of inverted pairs (\(a_i > a_j\) where \(i < j\)) in state \(q\), therefore \(X(q) \in \mathbb{N}\).
  • The state machine terminates because \(X(q)\) is strictly decreasing: for transition \(q \to r\), \(X(r) = X(q)-1\).
